content:
If you're great at what you do, but nobody knows, that's a "you" problem.

The market isn't going to discover you because you deserve it.

But, of course, someone half as talented is posting their work, explaining what they know, showing results, asking for the business, and getting paid.

Being uncomfortable with self-promotion is expensive.

But you don't need to become obnoxious.

You do need to get good at three things:

1. Show your work.

Talk about what you're building, what you're learning, what worked, and what failed. Be open, honest, and helpful.

2. Make your value extremely obvious.

Explain the problem you solve and show the result. Make it simple. A 6th-grader should be able to understand it.

3. Repeat yourself daily.

You are significantly more tired of your message than everyone else is. Most people missed it, forgot it, or are new to your world. Repeat!

People can't buy work they don't know exists.

And if you're building a one-person business, nobody else is coming to create that attention for you.

You have to learn how to get attention, earn trust, make good decisions, and turn your skills into income without spending your entire life doing it.

That took me years to figure out.

I wrote down everything I learned in a free solopreneur guide.

Hundreds of articles, hours of voice notes, and interviews with successful builders compressed into something you can read in less than 30 minutes.

content:
Most entrepreneurs try to build a business first and then cram their life around it.

I think that's a mistake.

Before you build anything, you should decide what your business is going to make possible in your life.

Here are some important questions to think through:

How many hours do you want to work?
How much income is actually enough?
Do you want weekends protected?
Do you want employees?
Do you want meetings?
Do you want to travel?

Those answers should help shape the business model that you eventually choose.

Because the answers affect what you sell, how you price it, how much complexity you install, and what kinds of customers you avoid.

You can build a "great" business and still build the wrong one for the life you want to live.

So define your life first.
Then build the business that supports it.

That was how I approached my one-person business, and it forced me to get excellent at a handful of skills:

Choosing the best work for me.
Keeping everything overly simple.
Protecting my time (especially weekends).
Creating predictable income with automation.
And growing without adding any complexity.

I learned so many lessons building my business this way. 

I took 7 of the most important ones and broke them down in a free 30-page guide on how I built my one-person business to $15M in profit.

It's hundreds of articles, hours of voice notes, and interviews with successful friends compressed into a short guide you can read in less than 30 minutes.

The most dangerous opportunities are the ones that look obviously good.

More reach.
More status.
More money.
More security.

The upside is so easy to see sitting right there in front of you.

The cost? Not so much.

That’s where I've found that people get themselves into a lot of trouble.

Because once an opportunity gets big enough, you can make almost any compromise sound reasonable.

You start to renegotiate your own priorities.
You explain away the thing you said mattered.
You convince yourself that this one is different.

Sometimes it is...

But sometimes you’re about to trade away something infinitely more valuable than what you’re getting back.

And the worst part is that you usually won’t know until much, much later.

I wrote about that problem in this week’s Saturday Essay.

It starts with one of the hardest "No's" I’ve ever come across.

Read about it below.

content:
Comfort is overrated.

A lot of people want a life of coasting.

Easy work.
Easy money.
Easy decisions.
Easy schedules.

After a while, they just wake up feeling miserable.

Some of my best moments in life came from doing things that sucked.

Building skills I was terrible at.
Building a business nobody cared about.
Showing up when results were disappointing.
Making decisions I wasn't completely sure about.

The point isn't to remove pain from your life.

It's to choose difficulty that actually makes your life better.

True in life...true in business.

Do hard work, feel crappy for a bit, and reap the rewards of being out of your comfort zone.

It took me a decade to get even mildly decent at it.

Eventually, I put together a little field guide on the stuff I learned.

Thousands of things I wrote, hours of voice notes, interviews with crazy successful people...

All condensed down to a guide you can read in 30 minutes.

Your job thinks you’re worth more than they’re paying you.

That’s just how business works. 

You get a little stability, some benefits, and a predictable paycheck. 

They get to keep the upside.

There's nothing wrong with that at all. 
It's been working like that for centuries.

I did it for 16 years and enjoyed it.

But there's a big mistake some people make.

They spend 20-30 years becoming more valuable and never even dip their toe in the water to find out whether their skills work in the market on their own.

At some point, you should at least run the experiment.

Can you solve a valuable problem?
Will someone pay you handsomely for it? 
Can you do it without blowing up your life?

If you find out the answer is yes, then you have to figure out how to turn that skill into income without letting it take over your life.

I spent nearly a decade figuring that out while building my one-person business to $15M.

Then I went back through hundreds of articles, hours of voice notes, and interviews with successful friends and narrowed everything I learned down to seven lessons every entrepreneur should understand.

There are three important decisions that have an outsized impact on your life.

1. Who you marry

Who you marry isn't only about the best of times.

It's also about your support system in the most difficult times.

All in all, probably the most important decision you can make.

2. Where you live

The place you call home should align with your energy and the type of community you want to build.

Love that city chaos? Get in there.
Need that quiet country serenity? Find it.
Need both? Try your best to split your time.

3. How you earn a living

There's nothing worse than building a business that you hate working in.

A business can make you rich and still be a terrible business for you.

If it requires 80-hour weeks, some giant team you never wanted, or spending a ton of your time doing work you hate, money doesn't magically make that a good deal.

I always wanted something different.

A business that earned extremely well, stayed simple, and left me enough time and energy for the rest of my life.

Figuring out how to actually build that took me a decade.

The 24/7 grinders won't experience the joy of a relaxed weekend with their spouse.

What a tragedy.

What's the point of doing all of this work if you never get the joy of downtime?

"Rise and grind."
"I'll sleep when I'm dead."

Lol. OK.

There's nothing wrong with hard work. I love working hard.

And there's nothing wrong with the occasional all-nighter or tough week, or workaholic month.

I get that. I've been there, too.

But if your identity is that work always gets 100% of your time, you're going to be a very sad and lonely person as you age.

If I could give one piece of advice to any aspiring entrepreneur, it would be this:

Build your life first and your business second.

Envision exactly how you want to live. What do your months, weeks, and days look like?

Then, fill in the gaps with exactly how work can support it.

content:
I just turned 34! 🎂 I LEARNT A LOT this year... Here are 3 things that might help ya 👇🏾

🔋 1. Energy is the foundational currency of life. 

I recently interviewed the leading mitochondria expert and the neuroscientist who popularised the idea of our finite daily "body budget." 

In this very noisy season of my life, every distraction, opportunity (they look the same), or social media scroll presents a temptation to spend my energy unproductively and unintentionally.

Once I fully appreciated that energy is THE finite biological currency - the centre point of my influence - determining everything I care about (family, business, health) - I became much more careful about where I placed my thoughts, as my thoughts direct my energy and I became much more diligent about what I say YES to!

After all, the biggest risk to a GREAT idea is energy wasted on lots of GOOD ones!

Becoming a master of "NO" is mission-critical and it's a skill the greatest entrepreneurs I've ever met all seem to have.

(Plus, I hope to become a dad soon, so I better get good at saying NO before a kid arrives!)

⏰ 2. The magical power of long-term thinking. 

A single 39-year-old friend recently told me, "Steven, I absolutely do NOT want to be dating this time next year." 

Unknowingly, when he said this, his goal shifted from "find someone to love" to "find the best person available before the 12-month clock runs out." - two very different goals.

He'll likely rush, overlook red flags, and repeat his cycle. 

This is the paradox of short-term thinking: we often waste time trying to save time. 

Often, the SLOW way is the FAST way, because the slow way is the ONLY way. 

A thought experiment: if I gave you unlimited bricks and 10 seconds to build a tower, you'd stack them vertically, only for a gust of wind to knock it down. 

If I gave you 1 year, you'd lay them horizontally, making a wide boring foundation and build a tower ten times taller that is built to last!

The point here is that, the time horizon you apply will change your decisions today, and today's decisions change your outcomes tomorrow.

This is long-term thinking - the ultimate (but increasingly rare) life-hack, in a world where people think about their life in 5 year segments.

By thinking in decades instead, my decisions across every area of my life I care about, have changed drastically.

So, I now endeavour to be impatient with the short term (move as fast as I can today), and patient with the long term (my long term goals).

The Romans has a phrase for this: festina lente (Make haste... slowly).

🎉 3. Catch the good old days in the act. 

The tragedy of "the good old days" is we rarely notice them while we're in them. We have to call them out! 

At 34, I'm doing work I love, surrounded by people I love. 

I am in the middle of the good old days. 

Thank you so much for the birthday messages! ❤️ 😊

content:
Only 3 in 10 Americans socialise on a daily basis.

So how good are we ACTUALLY at talking to each other anymore?

Vanessa Van Edwards believes we’re living through a “connection crisis”, where conversations are becoming harder, more awkward and less satisfying, while more of our interactions are moving away from real face-to-face conversation.

Vanessa is a behavioural researcher, international bestselling author and instructor at Harvard University whose work studies how people communicate, connect and understand each other.

And she said something to me early in this conversation that really stayed with me: people who invest in conversation skills now are creating “career insurance”.

She has spent years studying why some conversations seem effortless, why others die within minutes and what the best conversationalists are doing differently.

We discussed things like:

- Why “how are you?” and “what do you do?” can lead to dead-end conversations.
- The 3 levels of conversation and how to move from small talk into real connection.
- How awkward silence is one of our biggest conversational fears.
- The questions that reveal someone’s values, motivations and personality.
- 5 self-narratives that can influence how someone behaves at work and in relationships.
- Why becoming better at conversation could become increasingly valuable as AI changes how we communicate.

I’ve now had hundreds of conversations for this show and something Vanessa made me think about is that the best conversationalists are constantly paying attention to the person in front of them.

They aren’t blindly working through the things they want to say. They’re watching, listening and adjusting.

That sounds obvious until you start noticing how rarely people actually do it…

Vanessa has a way of breaking human connection down into things you can actually practise, which is probably why every time we speak I leave noticing things about my own behaviour that I hadn’t noticed before.

If you want to become better at talking to people, building relationships and having conversations people actually remember, I really recommend watching this one.

content:
I just turned 34! 🎂 I LEARNT A LOT this year... Here are 3 things that might help ya 👇🏾

🔋 1. Energy is the foundational currency of life. 

I recently interviewed the leading mitochondria expert and the neuroscientist who popularised the idea of our finite daily "body budget." 

In this very noisy season of my life, every distraction, opportunity (they look the same), or social media scroll presents a temptation to spend my energy unproductively and unintentionally.

Once I fully appreciated that energy is THE finite biological currency - the centre point of my influence - determining everything I care about (family, business, health) - I became much more careful about where I placed my thoughts, as my thoughts direct my energy and I became much more diligent about what I say YES to!

After all, the biggest risk to a GREAT idea is energy wasted on lots of GOOD ones!

Becoming a master of "NO" is mission-critical and it's a skill the greatest entrepreneurs I've ever met all seem to have.

(Plus, I hope to become a dad soon, so I better get good at saying NO before a kid arrives!)

⏰ 2. The magical power of long-term thinking. 

A single 39-year-old friend recently told me, "Steven, I absolutely do NOT want to be dating this time next year." 

Unknowingly, when he said this, his goal shifted from "find someone to love" to "find the best person available before the 12-month clock runs out." - two very different goals.

He'll likely rush, overlook red flags, and repeat his cycle. 

This is the paradox of short-term thinking: we often waste time trying to save time. 

Often, the SLOW way is the FAST way, because the slow way is the ONLY way. 

A thought experiment: if I gave you unlimited bricks and 10 seconds to build a tower, you'd stack them vertically, only for a gust of wind to knock it down. 

If I gave you 1 year, you'd lay them horizontally, making a wide boring foundation and build a tower ten times taller that is built to last!

The point here is that, the time horizon you apply will change your decisions today, and today's decisions change your outcomes tomorrow.

This is long-term thinking - the ultimate (but increasingly rare) life-hack, in a world where people think about their life in 5 year segments.

By thinking in decades instead, my decisions across every area of my life I care about, have changed drastically.

So, I now endeavour to be impatient with the short term (move as fast as I can today), and patient with the long term (my long term goals).

The Romans has a phrase for this: festina lente (Make haste... slowly).

🎉 3. Catch the good old days in the act. 

The tragedy of "the good old days" is we rarely notice them while we're in them. We have to call them out! 

At 34, I'm doing work I love, surrounded by people I love. 

I am in the middle of the good old days. 

Thank you so much for the birthday messages! ❤️ 😊

content:
The first 30 minutes after waking up could shape your entire day.

By the time you’re exhausted at night, your brain may be operating very differently.

Andrew Huberman put it simply: “Don’t say things tired.”

When we’re exhausted, our impulse control gets worse. The message you want to send, the argument you want to have or the decision that suddenly feels urgent can look completely different after some sleep.

That was one of many moments in this conversation that made me realise how much is happening inside our brains and bodies without us really understanding it.

Andrew is a neuroscientist and professor at Stanford, and what I value about speaking to him is that he goes beyond the simple health headlines and explains what is actually happening underneath them.

Cortisol isn’t simply “bad”. Ozempic isn’t only about weight loss. And some of the smallest things we do every day can have a surprisingly large effect on how we sleep, think and feel.

We covered things like:

- The 10 protocols to become the healthiest version of yourself
- When cortisol is actually good for you
- The eye movement trick that could help you fall asleep
- A neuroscientist’s perspective on God and religion
- The simple trick that can lower blood sugar spikes

One thing that really stayed with me was just how adaptable our brains are.

Andrew explained that repeatedly doing things you don’t want to do can physically change an area of the brain associated with tenacity. It made me look differently at the workout I want to skip, the difficult conversation I’m avoiding and those moments where choosing discomfort might actually prepare me for whatever comes next.

That’s why I enjoy conversations with Andrew. You leave with practical things you can use immediately but also ideas that change how you think about your own behaviour.

This conversation definitely did that for me.

I think it might for you too.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾 The Diary Of A CEO

content:
How do you process failure, and move on from it? 

My answer is quite simple: learn the lesson, then move on. I’ve realised that dwelling on failure rarely makes the next idea any better.

A lesser-known example of mine was the launch of Event magazine. It was our version of a “what’s on" magazine that we launched in the early 1980s. The logic seemed sound: we were already an entertainment business, so a culture magazine felt like a natural extension. 

But it came up against Time Out, which was already proving extremely successful, and Event simply couldn’t compete. We really thought we had spotted a great opportunity, but it just didn’t work. We quickly shut it down and learnt a very important lesson: Always protect the wider brand from one company’s failure. Then we moved on. 

My mum used to say, “Don’t cry over spilt milk”, and that has always stayed with me. 

Of course, you will feel deflated and, to be honest, an immense amount of stress. Digging deep into it won’t make that any easier. Work out what went wrong and write down what you’ve learnt (this part is important). Then put your energy into what comes next.

As I’ve always said: Business opportunities are like buses, there’s always another one coming. Just make sure you’re not looking in the rearview mirror.

#Failure #Lessons #Mindset

content:
“Eso lo maneja Calidad.”

Hay una frase que es muy común al interior de las organizaciones, pero que hacé más ruido aún durante una auditoría, cuando el auditor pregunta por un indicador y el responsable responde que lo tiene Calidad.
 
Pregunta por los riesgos del proceso y nuevamente: Eso lo maneja Calidad.
Pregunta cómo se hace seguimiento al desempeño, qué acciones se han tomado o dónde están determinadas ciertas actividades… y la respuesta vuelve a ser la misma.
 
¿Qué está pasando aquí?
 
Que posiblemente tenemos un sistema de gestión que está siendo administrado por Calidad, pero no necesariamente gestionado por quienes son responsables de los procesos.
 
Y son cosas muy diferentes.  Calidad puede acompañar. El proceso debe ser gestionado por su responsable.
 
El responsable de Calidad puede orientar metodologías, facilitar herramientas, consolidar información, hacer seguimiento al sistema, acompañar a los procesos y promover la mejora.
 
Pero quien lidera un proceso debería poder explicar, como mínimo:
🔹 ¿Cuál es el propósito de su proceso?
🔹 ¿Cuáles son sus principales riesgos y controles?
🔹 ¿Qué resultados debe alcanzar?
🔹 ¿Cómo sabe si está funcionando?
🔹 ¿Qué problemas ha identificado?
🔹 ¿Qué decisiones o mejoras ha implementado?
🔹 ¿Qué evidencias puede demostrar?

Si para responder estas preguntas siempre necesitamos acudir a Calidad, estamos ante un riesgo importante:  el sistema de gestión funciona… pero funciona depende exclusivamente de Calidad.
 
Los responsables terminan viendo los indicadores como “los indicadores de Calidad”, los riesgos como “la matriz que hizo Calidad”, las auditorías como “algo que revisa Calidad” y las acciones de mejora como “tareas que pidió Calidad”.
 
Y entonces el sistema deja de ser una herramienta para gestionar la organización y se convierte en un sistema paralelo que alguien debe mantener.
 
Una auditoría puede ayudarnos a detectar esto, pregúntate: 
“¿Cómo está funcionando mi proceso respecto al Sistema de Gestión?”
 
Un proceso realmente maduro no depende de que alguien de Calidad esté al lado para explicar y sus resultados y funcionamiento.
 
El responsable conoce su proceso, conoce sus resultados, conoce sus problemas, y  participa en sus decisiones y mejoras.
 
Calidad no es quien responde por todos los procesos, es quien ayuda a que cada proceso tenga la capacidad de responder por sí mismo.
 
La calidad no es responsabilidad de Calidad, es responsabilidad de quienes hacen y gestionan los procesos.
 
Si mañana Calidad no estuviera en la reunión, ¿podrías explicar cómo está funcionando tu proceso?

OpenAI just dropped GPT-6 ASTRA!!! 🚀✨

We’ve been testing it extensively at Every Inc. across coding, writing, and knowledge work. My take: it’s a big upgrade from 5.6-Sol, with some frustrating habits that keep it from matching Fable at the top end.

Here’s your vibe check:

- The best writing model I’ve tried. It’s fast, produces very little slop, and is easy to steer. It’s a good companion for actually working through the writing I do every day. (Not to mention, it one-shotted the first draft of its own vibe check today!)

- The computer use is wild. It can go for hours at a time using complicated apps to get work done. It did the first cut of our Fable 5.1 vibe check video...kind of mindblowing

- Impressive 3D games and visualizations. It can make beautiful 3D worlds from a single prompt. I one-shotted a historically accurate rendition of the Battle of Waterloo

- It can overcomplicate things. (Especially at higher effort levels.) Ask for a simple interface and you get extra labels, buttons, and features everywhere. It has a habit of turning everything into a landing page.

It just doesn't quite match Fable's ability to intuitively understand your prompt and do something delightful (without overcomplicating.)

Net Result:

content:
"We are transitioning from a knowledge economy to an allocation economy."

That was the insight that Vijay Khatri, Dean at the Leeds School of Business, shared after my keynote last night on campus for a YPO event. 

He was building on my perspective about what it takes to achieve AI fluency. One of the building blocks was knowing when to use artificial intelligence and when to have a human do the work.

Whether it's leadership thinking about allocation of work tasks or whether it's individual contributors making that fork-in-the-road decision, it's important. 

He and I spent time talking about it and I was enlightened by his point of view. We discussed  how the knowledge economy was based on knowing and utilizing knowledge at the right time, but with AI's great leap, machines could handle much of that load. 

In this new economy the leader's role is to manage the allocation of work to machines, keeping the essentially human skills (taste, goal setting, talent evaluation) in order to deliver more strategic work. 

For a primer on this concept read Dan Shipper's groundbreaking essay (Welcome to the Allocation Economy). Link  ⬇️. 

In 2024, Shipper realized that his knowledge skill of summarizing could be done efficiently by ChatGPT (even in its nascent state). So he allocated that to machines, transitioning from maker to manager. He checked on the work, improved his prompts and mastered this allocation pretty quickly. 

Likely, it was the first of many maker-to-manager transitions he went through, which made him a 10x manager (his company Every's success demonstrates how much revenue and value a small group of humans can produce.) 

I appreciate the prompt by Dean Khatri: AI fluency isn't just about being better at using a tool. It's about strategic allocation of work to a tool that's as fit (or better) to do the job. 

(PS - There's a recent academic paper in management science that argues that task allocation remains a human stronghold, despite the gains in generative AI. This is where the value of judgement comes into play. Link  ⬇️)

content:
Monday was Tim Cook's last day as CEO at Apple.

I first met Tim in 2014 and I've been fortunate to call him a mentor and friend ever since. I want to share something about him that I've found remarkable.

He's the best example I've seen of an old Zen saying:

"What do you do before enlightenment? Chop wood, carry water. What do you do after enlightenment? Chop wood, carry water."

When we met, I was just starting my career in finance. I was getting to the gym at 4:45am so I could get to the office by 6:30. Tim happened to be one of a tiny group of others who showed up every morning at that early hour.

For the first six months, I had no idea who he was. I wasn't in tech and, having played college sports, I was frankly quite oblivious to the entire business world.

I remember being shocked after someone told me that the guy I was talking to in the mornings was the CEO of Apple.

For two reasons:

1. He had zero pretension about him. I never would have known how important or powerful he was.

2. He was already successful. Why the hell was he waking up at 4am to go to the gym?

Now, to be fair, in 2014, there were still questions about whether he was going to be an impactful successor to the legend that was Steve Jobs. A lot of people weren't sure he would be able to fill those enormous shoes.

But a few years later, he was still there. He had created a trillion dollars of value. People were calling him one of the best CEOs in the world. And he was still showing up at 4:45am. Still doing the same thing.

Chop wood, carry water.

As you start to experience success, notoriety, and achievement, it’s easy to lose sight of the work that got you those things in the first place. It’s easy to get distracted by results. By recognition. By the illusion that success somehow exempts you from the basics.

It doesn’t.

The outcomes may change. The titles may change. The scale may change. But the work doesn’t.

Chopping wood and carrying water means showing up when no one is watching. Doing the boring work well. Being reliable. Executing consistently. Returning to fundamentals even when you think you’re above them. Especially then.

Tim has been an example of that in my life. I'm grateful for having been able to see it up close.

And I also know that whatever he does next, the same thing will apply.

Chop wood, carry water.

content:
A two-decade-old column changed how I see time.

(I used to think I was behind.)

In the year 2000, a man wrote to the Dear Abby advice column.

He said, "I'm a 36-year-old college dropout. My lifelong dream was to be a doctor. I have a good job selling pharmaceutical supplies, but my heart is still in medicine. If I go back to college, get my degree, go to medical school, do my internship, and finally start practicing, it'll take me seven years. In seven years, I'll be 43 years old. What do you think?"

Dear Abby's response: "And how old will you be in seven years if you don't go to medical school?"

Let that sink in.

When I read that, I flashed back to every single version of "it's too late" I've ever told myself.

Every story about being off track, behind, or lost.

Back to my late 20s when I felt like a failure while watching people post about their startup's funding round, their promotion, their Forbes 30 under 30 accolade.

All those times I longed for someone to come tap me in, tell me I was on track, tell me I was worthy.

But here's what it took me years to understand.

The timeline in my head was entirely invented.

My own creation, an abstraction so far removed from reality it didn't even resemble the real thing anymore.

We built these timelines from a young age.

We look at the world, scroll social media, and sketch out a map of how life is supposed to go.

What we should have done by 25, 35, and why we can't possibly start now.

We tie ourselves in knots.

We know what we really want, but we're too afraid to go all in because going all in means exposing yourself to real failure, being completely naked.

But here's the harsh truth Dear Abby nailed.

Time doesn't care about you.

It's moving with or without you, whether you act or not, whether you live the way you want or not.

Time is just going to pass.

And the research backs this up.

A Cornell University study found something powerful.

We regret our actions in the short term, but in the long term, we regret inaction.
It's never the things we did that haunt us, it's the things we didn't do.

Here's my question to you: How often do we all sit around waiting for someone else to come tap us into our own life?

To give us permission to go and do the thing we want to do.

The real lesson here is recognizing you don't need any of that.

You don't need permission. You don't need a Dear Abby column. You don't 
need this video.

You need to just tap yourself in.

You get to choose.

You're not late, you're not early, you're exactly where your life has led you to be.

And you get to decide where you go from here.

That thing you want to do, how old will you be in seven years if you don't?

——

content: It feels like we are entering a period where things change faster than we can settle our opinions about them. Something can look impossible, then impressive, then ordinary within a few months. Tools keep getting cheaper as models get better, and work that once needed a team or years of accumulated skill can suddenly be attempted by one person on a Tuesday afternoon. That does something strange to our sense of value. As building gets easier and information becomes abundant, even intelligence begins to feel less scarce. Judgment gets harder to fake. You have to notice what changed, figure out what matters, and stay with a problem long enough to understand it before the next thing arrives. AI also seems to be speeding up the feedback loop around technology itself. A new capability changes how people behave, which changes what they expect from products and from each other. Those expectations become the input to the next round of software and ways of working, and the gaps between each turn keep getting shorter. I think we are still learning how to live inside that. Maybe the useful skill is staying oriented while the environment keeps moving, trying things early enough to learn from them, and updating your beliefs without rebuilding your worldview every week. The world can move fast without forcing your judgment to move at the same speed.

Another AI milestone has been hit: Google DeepMind’s new AlphaGenome Atlas has predicted the biological effects of all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome, which will help researchers understand genetic diseases.

This is an amazing achievement, but predicting the effects of genetic mutations is not the same as curing disease. And there’s a big reason why: human nature. An estimated 80% of chronic diseases and premature deaths are not driven by our genes — but rather by the way we live: what we eat, how much we move, how we sleep, how we manage stress and how we stay socially connected.

This latest feat will no doubt dramatically speed up medical advances and improve many lives, but we still need to focus on what we’ve known long before AI: that making even small changes in our daily behaviors can have a profound and proven impact on health outcomes.

content:
One word stands out to me in a remarkable new study from Eli Lilly and Company: persistent.

The study, published in "Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism," followed nearly 16,000 adults over 55 who started Lilly’s injectable weight management medication — matched with similar adults who were not on treatment. Over 18 months, persistent users who stayed on the treatment had fewer hospital and emergency room visits than the untreated group. Their healthcare costs also grew more slowly.

That’s the power of persistence. And it’s just as true for our daily behaviors — food, movement, sleep, stress management and connection — as it is for medication adherence. Medicines plus healthy habits create outcomes that neither can achieve alone.

And maybe that's this part of the conversation.”
 
Then, later in the day, I was listening to Ezra Klein’s re-run of an interview with the legendary music producer Rick Rubin, which had an uncanny echo to Huberman's. “Before we started this together,” said Rubin. “I did a ritual for us where I envisioned my higher self floating above me. And I envisioned you, and I envisioned your higher self floating above you. It's nearly time for the annual Microsoft Be Well Games, powered by Thrive Global. We're building on the remarkable success of last year's Games, bringing the global challenge to more than 190,000 employees — along with their family and a few friends — from September 8th to October 6th, in a way that goes far beyond a traditional fitness challenge. Because wellbeing isn't one-size-fits-all. It means something different to each of us. That's why the Be Well Games take a holistic approach, grounded in the five foundational daily behaviors that govern our health: food, movement, sleep, stress management and connection.

What makes these behaviors so powerful is that they compound. Small, sustainable habits — a short walk between meetings, a real lunch break, a consistent bedtime, a moment to reset before a hard conversation — allow us to show up as our best, most productive, most creative selves. Because when you feel your best, you perform at your best: not just at work, but at home, and in the things that matter most to you. The Be Well Games remind us that wellbeing isn't a trade-off against performance. It's the foundation of it.

And connection is where it all comes together. As people across the company work toward 8,000 minutes of wellbeing activities, it's not just about logging numbers and winning prizes — it's about the human connections that are the most powerful drivers of lasting habit change. We're far more likely to stick with a new habit when someone is walking alongside us. The Be Well Games are an opportunity to improve individual wellbeing while finding support, camaraderie, and community — across teams, time zones, and kitchen tables.

Amy Coleman, Microsoft's Chief People Officer, puts it this way: “Performance and well-being aren't in competition. In fact, taking care of ourselves is how we do our best work. The small habits we stick with, day after day, can make the biggest difference.”

Here's to a month of building habits that last — together.

September is Blood Cancer Awareness Month. And our new project in partnership with Bristol Myers Squibb is offering support to people living with cancer, including multiple myeloma, a rare blood cancer without a cure.

Together, Thrive Global and BMS launched Thriving Through Multiple Myeloma, a free wellbeing resource for people living with multiple myeloma and those caring for them. The site, Myeloma Central, provides practical daily guidance on eating well, moving more, sleeping better, managing stress, and staying connected. As the science shows, these foundational behaviors are critical for managing chronic disease and health in general. We’ve launched with a selection of articles, short videos, and Thrive Resets, designed to support people living with the condition alongside resources for people living with other types of cancer.

While no two multiple myeloma journeys are the same, many patients experience similar challenges. For example, almost everyone with the disease experiences a relapse, and even though this is a normal and expected part of the journey, hearing the news can still be devastating. It’s a moment that can bring distress, anxiety, and uncertainty, which makes it a moment when the right support can have a real impact. Our resources help patients navigate that uncertainty and take small steps in areas such as eating for bone strength, getting adequate sleep while experiencing bone pain, and building a multiple myeloma support circle.

With the recent approval of BMS's first CELMoD therapy for multiple myeloma, this partnership exemplifies one of our core beliefs that also is backed by an increasing number of studies: that medicines plus healthy habits can create outcomes that neither can achieve alone. And this rollout is just the beginning.

Thank you to BMS, Chris Boerner, Wendy Bartie, and Monica Shaw.

We need a cure for AI health hype. “I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years,” wrote Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei recently on X. And on 60 Minutes last year, Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Google DeepMind, declared that “we can cure all disease with the help of Al… maybe within the next decade or so, I don’t see why not.”

Actually, there’s a big reason why not: human nature. An estimated 80% of chronic diseases and premature deaths are not driven by our genes — but rather by the way we live: what we eat, how much we move, how we sleep, how we manage stress and how we stay socially connected. The current debate on AI curing all diseases is more than a tempest in a GPTeapot — it points to a larger problem: so much of the conversation is focused on improving the machines, and so little on investing energy and resources on improving humans.

You can read more in my latest newsletter On My Mind. 

Plus, yiayia hobbies, why you should be fiber-maxxing, an undersea lesson on love, and my nightstand takes on the “end of reading.”

content:
AI models have jumped containment but our collective conversation about AI is far too contained. This week another set of frontier AI models was set for release, with announcements for the upcoming launch of OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1.
 
In a post on X about Astra, Sam Altman wrote about how “the world will need aligned AI” and that “an iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.” 

He talks about society, but what is society? Society consists not just of institutions but individuals. For society to evolve, individuals have to evolve, but what are we asking of ourselves? That’s the part of the AI conversation we never get to.
 
“Evolve together” seems to mostly mean humans accommodating themselves to AI as it gets better and better. But why are we assuming machines can keep getting better but humans can't? 

As we work toward recursive self-improvement in machines, we seem to have lost sight of the recursive self-improvement that’s built into our humanity. We’re born to evolve — not as a metaphor or a self-help slogan, but as an imperative built into our design.
 
And yet as the AI models become more powerful, the humans in the equation seem to become less powerful and have less agency. Of course safety is important, but it’s not the only part of the conversation that matters. Thriving is about more than just avoiding the worst-case scenario.
 
“AI is getting extremely capable,” Altman wrote. But as AI is becoming more capable, we need just as much focus on how humans can become more capable. Evolving together has to mean more than just watching AI become more powerful and accommodating ourselves to it. 

Society evolves only when its members evolve.

content:
Good morning fams💯😁

It’s a new week again.Absolutely. Let’s talk about productivity

What is productivity?

Productivity is not simply about doing more work. It is about using your time, energy, skills, and resources effectively to achieve meaningful results.

For a business owner or freelancer, productivity means being intentional about what you do instead of just staying busy.

5 important areas of productivity

1. Set clear goals 🎯
    Know exactly what you want to achieve. A clear goal makes it easier to know what deserves your attention.

2. Prioritize your tasks
    Not every task is equally important. Focus first on activities that directly contribute to your business growth, income, clients, or skills.

3. Manage your time ⏰
    Create a simple schedule for your day. Give specific periods to work, learning, communication, and rest.

4. Avoid distractions
    Social media, unnecessary conversations, and constantly checking your phone can consume a lot of productive time. Learn to protect your focus.

5. Review your progress 📈
    At the end of the day or week, ask yourself:
    What did I accomplish? What didn’t I finish? What can I do better next time?

Productivity in business

For a freelancer, productivity could look like:

Plan → Create → Deliver → Communicate → Learn → Review

The goal isn’t to work 24/7. The goal is to make sure the hours you spend working are actually moving you and your business forward.

A busy person is not always a productive person. Productivity is measured by results, not just activity.

content:
Here’s probably an unpopular opinion:

Cell phones are killing productivity in the work center.

When I started my military career, I spent my first 16 years working in secure facilities where personal cell phones simply weren’t an option. You showed up, you worked, you communicated with the people around you, and you went home.

When I eventually transitioned back into work centers where people had access to their phones, I noticed something I hadn’t fully appreciated before:

The level of distraction and the resulting loss in productivity was significant.

It wasn’t always one big distraction. It was the constant little ones.

A text message. A social media notification. Checking the weather. Scrolling for a few minutes. Responding to something that could have waited. Then doing it again 20 minutes later.

At one point, I even had a commander question why I had a box sitting in the work center for people to place their phones in.

My answer was simple:

Because the phones had become too much of a distraction, and I could see the impact on productivity.

I’m not against cell phones. They’re incredibly useful tools, and there are absolutely legitimate reasons to have them available.

But I’ve come to believe that “having access to your phone” and “needing your phone at work” are two very different things.

Maybe I’m old school, but I don’t believe personal cell phones belong in most work centers.

Give people a place to focus, eliminate unnecessary distractions, and let them do what we hired/trained them to do.

What do you think? Are cell phones improving the modern workplace—or quietly destroying productivity?

content:
I’ve been quietly building something for months, and I think it’s time I started talking about it publicly.
It began because I had a problem I couldn’t seem to solve with ordinary productivity systems.
I don’t have trouble generating ideas. I have trouble preserving everything that made an idea make sense when it appeared.
A note can preserve the sentence.
A task manager can preserve the action.
A folder can preserve the document.
But none of those necessarily preserve the thought—what led to it, what it connected to, what changed along the way, what was rejected, what remained unresolved, and why the final decision made sense.
I needed a way to leave something and come back days or months later without reconstructing my own brain from scratch.
So I started building one.
What began as a way to manage my journalism, career work and an increasingly ridiculous number of interconnected ideas has turned into something much larger: a system for preserving context and continuity across work.
The principle underneath it is simple:
You should be able to find your way back to the thought on command.
I’m still building it. I’m still testing where it breaks. And I’m deliberately not explaining all of it yet.
But I’m done pretending I’m not building it just because it isn’t finished.
More soon.

Busy Doesn't Always Mean Productive

One of the biggest misunderstandings in hospitality is confusing being busy with being productive.

A restaurant can be full.

A kitchen can be running nonstop.

A hotel can have 95% occupancy.

And the operation can still be inefficient.

If employees are constantly searching for supplies, repeating tasks, waiting for information, correcting mistakes or dealing with avoidable guest issues, people may be extremely busy but the operation isn't necessarily performing well.

There is a difference between:

Activity and productivity.

Activity asks:

How much are we doing?

Productivity asks:

How effectively are we doing it?

Sometimes the solution isn't hiring more people.

Sometimes it is fixing the process.

Better communication.

Clearer responsibilities.

Smarter preparation.

Better forecasting.

Less unnecessary movement.

In hospitality efficiency isn't about making people work harder.

It is about removing the things that make good people work harder than necessary.

content:
Remote work solved a lot of problems for business owners. And quietly created a few new ones nobody really planned for.

The one I hear most: nobody knows who's available, who's on a call, or who dropped the ball on following up with a customer, because everyone's working from a different location on a different setup and the communication stack was never built for it.

When your team was all in one office, you could look up and see who was on the phone. You could tap someone on the shoulder for a handoff. Now that same handoff goes through three texts, a missed call, and a Slack message that got buried under 40 others.

Hybrid and remote teams need communication infrastructure that actually reflects how they work, not a system designed for a physical office that no longer exists.

The businesses that figured that out early are running a lot smoother than the ones still patching it together.

Remote work: what people think it is vs. what it actually is. 😂

What people think:
☕ Wake up whenever you want.
👚 Work in pajamas all day.
📺 Netflix playing in the background.
🧺 Get all the laundry and housework done between emails.
😌 Basically get paid to hang out at home.

🎧 Back-to-back meetings while your coffee gets cold beside you.
📧 Emails. Teams messages. Reports. Deadlines. More Teams messages.
🏠 Being physically at home while accomplishing approximately ZERO things for your home.
😂 Someone in your family saying, “Since you’re home…” and immediately testing your patience.

It takes discipline, time management, communication, accountability, and the ability to stay productive without someone physically standing over your shoulder.

And honestly? Remote work has taught me a lot about myself professionally. It’s pushed me to communicate better, manage my time more intentionally, solve problems independently, and understand that productivity isn’t about where someone’s desk is — it’s about what they accomplish from it.

So yes, I work from home.

• Strong operating rhythms

Remote work requires stronger governance, not less accountability.

When the operating model is clear, remote teams can deliver exceptional results.

The question should not be, “Can people be productive remotely?”

We’re spending millions on AI watermarking and detection tools.

I think we’re fortifying a door in a wall that’s about to come down.

The entire detection model rests on a temporary assumption: AI is something we can meaningfully opt into or out of, something separate from “normal” work.

I contend that this assumption has an expiration date.

When intelligence is built into the operating system, the device, the applications, and every step of the workflow, “Did you use AI?” may eventually sound like “Did you use electricity?”

I made a short video tracing the five stages that lead us there, ending with what I call Ambient Intelligence: the phase in which the interface disappears and intelligence becomes part of the environment itself.

Watch the attached video. Then tell me: Are we preparing people for the world that’s arriving, or policing the one that’s already fading?

content:
AI, machine learning, and deep learning are often used interchangeably.
But they’re not the same thing.
The easiest way to understand them is as a hierarchy:
Artificial Intelligence → Machine Learning → Deep Learning
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the broadest category.
It refers to systems designed to perform tasks that normally require human-like intelligence—such as recognizing patterns, understanding language, solving problems, or making decisions.

Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI.

Instead of programming every rule by hand, we give a machine learning system data so it can learn patterns and use them to make predictions or decisions.
Deep Learning (DL) is a subset of machine learning.

It uses multi-layered neural networks to learn more complex patterns from data. Deep learning powers many of the advances behind modern image recognition, speech recognition, and generative AI.

So:
AI
↳ Machine Learning
↳ Deep Learning

The key distinction:

All deep learning is machine learning.

All machine learning is AI.

But not all AI is machine learning, and not all machine learning is deep learning.

Once you understand that relationship, a lot of AI terminology starts making much more sense.

How far has AI actually come?

We often talk about “AI” as if it's one thing.
It isn't.

AI can be thought of across different levels:

Reactive AI - Responds to inputs without memory.
Limited Memory AI - Uses past data to improve decisions.
Reasoning AI - Analyzes information, identifies patterns, and makes predictions.
Theory of Mind AI - A theoretical form of AI that could understand human emotions, intentions, and beliefs.
Self-Aware AI - Theoretical AI capable of understanding its own existence.

And then there's robotics, where AI moves from processing information to physically interacting with the world.

The interesting question isn't just:

“How intelligent is AI?”

It's:

“What happens when AI becomes capable of reasoning, acting autonomously, and making decisions that affect us?”

That's where AI stops being just a technology conversation.

It becomes a conversation about privacy, cybersecurity, safety, accountability, and governance.

Where do you think we are on this spectrum today?

THE LIMITS AND LEVERS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
  
Artificial intelligence is metamorphically “a brilliant servant and a questionable master”
  
Artificial intelligence may be the most impressive intern humanity has ever hired; fast, fantastic but occasionally faulty and failing.
  
That contradiction captures the limits and levers of artificial intelligence.
  
The lever is extraordinary. Artificial intelligence can dramatically reduce the cost of turning human intentions into compelling output.
  
In a controlled MIT empirical study involving 453 professionals, access to generative artificial intelligence reduced completion time on writing tasks by about 40% while improving quality of output by 18%. Stanford`s AI index similarly reports that more than 78% of organisations used artificial intelligence in 2025, up from 55% in 2023.
  
In other words, intelligence has become cheaper to rent, although renting intelligence is not the same as being innately smart or possessing depth of wisdom. 
  
I am convinced that the arc of the future is neither artificial intelligence versus humans. It is artificial intelligence with humans versus humans.
  
The winning formula could be depth of human intelligence enhanced by machine intelligence, producing an amplified capacity.
  
Artificial intelligence is the new horsepower, human will still seat in the cart and directs its trajectory…. history has a customary way of blinking!!

content:
THE LIMITS AND LEVERS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Artificial intelligence is metamorphically “a brilliant servant and a questionable master”

Artificial intelligence may be the most impressive intern humanity has ever hired; fast, fantastic but occasionally faulty and failing.

That contradiction captures the limits and levers of artificial intelligence.

The lever is extraordinary. Artificial intelligence can dramatically reduce the cost of turning human intentions into compelling output.

In a controlled MIT empirical study involving 453 professionals, access to generative artificial intelligence reduced completion time on writing tasks by about 40% while improving quality of output by 18%. Stanford`s AI index similarly reports that more than 78% of organisations used artificial intelligence in 2025, up from 55% in 2023.

In other words, intelligence has become cheaper to rent, although renting intelligence is not the same as being innately smart or possessing depth of wisdom.

I am convinced that the arc of the future is neither artificial intelligence versus humans. It is artificial intelligence with humans versus humans.

The winning formula could be depth of human intelligence enhanced by machine intelligence, producing an amplified capacity.

Artificial intelligence is the new horsepower, human will still seat in the cart and directs its trajectory…. history has a customary way of blinking!!

The AI Transition: Slow Down to Speed Up
There's a race happening right now — everyone trying to get to "first place" in the AI transition. As an early adopter myself, I'm genuinely an advocate for AI. But a line I read recently stopped me:

"Let AI handle more of the cruise control. We'll keep our hands near the wheel. Because the future of leadership isn't choosing between artificial intelligence and human intelligence. It's knowing when to use each."

That's the piece too many organizations are skipping.
Here's what I'd add, from an HR seat: when you eliminate entry-level positions to chase efficiency, you're not just cutting cost. You're cutting out the learning that happens in career progression — the reps, the mistakes, the mentorship that builds judgment over time.

And then, a few years out, you have a gap. Not a skills gap — a leadership readiness gap. Schools are adapting fast on technical skills. But leadership capability? That shift hasn't caught up yet.

AI can absolutely handle the cruise control. But we still need people who know how to drive — and we're not building enough of them if we skip the steps that taught the last generation how.

Artificial Intelligence, a concept we often associate with modern technology, has surprisingly old roots, originating in the 1940s and '50s.

Initially termed 'cybernetics,' pioneers in the field, including psychiatrists and doctors, explored how biological systems regulate themselves—like body temperature and blood sugar. They sought to replicate these self-regulating feedback loops using electrical signals.

Mathematicians later advanced this concept into computing, coining the term 'artificial intelligence' to distinguish it from its biological origins. This historical context reveals that AI was never solely about mimicking human-like intelligence, but rather about understanding and replicating complex regulatory systems. #ArtificialIntelligence #Cybernetics #HistoryOfAI #TechInnovation #FutureOfTech

content:
ANI, AGI, and ASI explained simply.

These three terms are often used in AI conversations, but they describe very different levels of intelligence.

→ ANI: Artificial Narrow Intelligence
This is the AI we use today. It is designed to perform a specific task very well, such as recommending videos, recognizing faces, translating text, or answering questions.

Tools like ChatGPT, Claude, recommendation systems, and image models fall into this broader narrow-AI world because they are built around defined capabilities.

→ AGI: Artificial General Intelligence
AGI would be able to understand, learn, adapt, and solve problems across many different domains at a human-like level.

Instead of being great at one category of task, it could transfer knowledge, reason across situations, and learn new skills with much more flexibility.

AGI does not exist yet.

→ ASI: Artificial Superintelligence
ASI goes one step further. It refers to intelligence that would surpass humans across areas like science, strategy, creativity, medicine, engineering, and decision-making.

This is still theoretical.

A simple way to remember it:

ANI = specialized intelligence
AGI = human-level general intelligence
ASI = beyond-human intelligence

A lot of AI conversations become easier once you know which level people are actually talking about.

After 30+ years in career development, I’m more careful about giving career advice than I was when I started.

I assumed experience would work the other way.

Learn enough theories.
Use enough assessments.
Coach enough people.
Eventually, you should get pretty good at knowing what people should do.

Thousands of career conversations taught me something different.

Follow your passion.
Play to your strengths.
Make a five-year plan.
Never burn a bridge.

I still believe there’s wisdom in all four.

But good advice gets into trouble when we start treating it like a rule.

These days, before I offer an answer, I’m much more likely to ask:

“What do we need to understand before you decide?”

I wrote this week’s newsletter about the career advice I’ve stopped giving the way I once did, and what 30+ years in this work changed my mind about.

Expertise isn’t always having the answer faster. Sometimes it’s knowing what you still need to understand before offering one.

content:
With the most recent summer associate class continuing on their journeys, and the new fall associate class starting soon, I have been asked frequently for early career advice. The first thing that comes to mind—not every opportunity is your opportunity.

That may sound counterintuitive early in your career, when the instinct is often to say yes to everything. And early on, broad experience matters. But over time, I’ve learned that the lawyers who build the most sustainable and rewarding careers are often the ones who become increasingly intentional about where they invest their time and energy.

My second piece of advice—play the long game.

Invest in relationships. Deliver excellent work consistently. Raise your hand for challenging opportunities. Build a reputation for being someone others want on their team. And most importantly, remember that careers are built over decades, not quarters.

The relationships you invest in, the reputation you build and the judgment you develop over time will shape your career far more than any single assignment, matter or promotion.

The worst thing you can do it take career advice from the people who love you.

I learned that the hard way when I left corporate to build my first business.

People around me had strong opinions about what I should do.

I get it...their fear was real to them.

It also belonged to their experience of the world.

I see the same dynamic with people I coach.

A spouse worried about income.
A parent thinking about security.
A friend comparing your decision.

While those perspectives may deserve respect, they also need to stay in their proper place because you are the person who will live inside the dcisions you make. Not them.

Advice can inform a decision.

It should never become permission.

When the people around you are nervous about your next move, listen for the information inside the fear.

Then make the decision you are willing to own.

content:
It’s so strange to want out of a career you're objectively good at.

If the job were a disaster, the decision would be easier. But the paycheck’s decent. You’ve built a reputation. And other people hear your title and think you’re doing well.

Meanwhile, you’re thinking, I don’t know if I want to do this anymore.

That’s hard to admit after spending years getting good at the work.

I hear this all the time. You know you need a change but can’t explain what kind. Or you’ve got 15 possible ideas and don’t trust any of them.

Wanting something different can feel ridiculous when nothing looks wrong from the outside. But that urge doesn’t come out of nowhere. 

Usually, your career has stopped meeting a need you may not have known you had.

Career change advice tends to start with the next job. Transferable skills, industries, networking, maybe even another degree.

All useful. But we’re skipping the question that should come first.

Why has this career stopped working for the person you've become?

content:
Career fair season is HERE — which means students everywhere are asking:
What do employers REALLY look for at career fairs? And how do I stand out when recruiters are meeting hundreds of students?

I have LOTS of opinions on this one. But I also have a bit of an obsession with career advice that starts with, “Here's what X is looking for in their candidates…”

Because...which recruiter? Which hiring manager? Which company? Which job?

We’re humans. We notice different things.

One hiring manager may love a perfectly polished elevator pitch. Another would much rather you forget the script and just have a genuine conversation. One cares about GPA. Another wants to hear about the project you worked on, the problem you solved, or what you're genuinely curious about.

There ARE some things that are pretty universal, though — preparation, curiosity, engagement, thoughtful questions and being able to tell your story.

So, I pulled together some of my favorite advice for students heading into career fair season -- but every manager I have ever chatted with has a different thing that they are looking for.

One piece of career advice I give often is this:

If there's an opportunity you genuinely want to be involved in, don't assume you have to wait for an invitation.

There are meetings and organizations where someone will ask:

“Is anyone interested?”

“Does anyone have an idea?”

“Would anyone like to help?”

Even if you're not a formal member, sometimes the best thing you can do is simply raise your hand.

Volunteering your time can be a valuable way to learn, contribute, and become involved.

You don't need to force yourself into every opportunity.

But when something genuinely aligns with your interests and career direction, don't let the absence of a formal title stop you from participating.

September is a month of new beginnings.

New jobs. New projects. New teams. New opportunities.

If I could give one piece of career advice to anyone starting something new, it would be this:

Listen. Listen. Listen.

Speak to people. Ask questions. Be curious.

You have two ears and one mouth for a reason! Use them accordingly.

Don’t feel you need to have all the answers from day one. Talk to people who have been there before. Ask questions. Listen to different perspectives. Seek clarity before jumping to conclusions.

You’ll learn more, build better relationships and make better decisions.

Sometimes, the best way to find your way forward is simply to listen to those around you.

article.description: When you are recovering from burnout or career depletion, you may not need a destination. You may only need a direction.This article is based on Chapt

content:
If you've spent months asking yourself "what do I actually want next," you're not overthinking. You're just missing the right exercise.

Most career clarity advice tells you to think harder, journal more, or wait until something feels obvious. That kind of certainty is never coming, and waiting for it is exactly what keeps you stuck.

There's a tool that came out of Stanford called Odyssey Planning, and it works because it stops asking you to find the one right answer.

Instead, you map out three completely different versions of your next five years. Three real paths you could actually see yourself living, not hypotheticals, not fantasies.

One is the life you're already on, played forward. One is what you'd do if that whole path disappeared tomorrow. And one is what you'd go after if money and everyone else's opinion were completely off the table.

When you put all three side by side, you stop staring at a blank page wondering what you want. You have actual options in front of you, and you can start to feel which one pulls you forward.

That's the difference between spinning and moving.

I'm breaking down exactly how to do this so subscribe to my substack: https://lnkd.in/ehQAratq.

Twenty years ago, I accepted a role in California without ever having set foot in the state.

I told my family it would be a couple of years. 

Each move since has meant a new company, often a new industry, and a network built from nothing. They're never comfortable. The growth that comes from these experiences is irreplaceable.

The advice I give every mentee about weighing a big move: Picture where you want to be in five years. Ask whether this path, however unconventional, gets you closer.

Then ask the harder version. Will you regret not taking it?

Every bold choice in my career came from the second question.

WEDNESDAY NEXT CHAPTER INSIGHT | CLARIFY

Something I hear often when talking with executives who are trying to figure out what’s next is the pressure to have an answer.

Do I want another executive role?

 Could I consult?

 Should I start something of my own?

 What about board work?

And my advice is usually: you don’t have to figure that out yet.

Start smaller.

Think about where you are right now and ask yourself:

What do I want MORE of in my next chapter?

 And what do I want LESS of?

Maybe it’s more autonomy and less bureaucracy.

More building and less maintaining.

More flexibility and less travel.

Don’t worry yet about what title, company, or career path gives you those things.

For now, just pay attention to what your answers are telling you.

So I'm curious about this group:
What's one thing you know you want MORE of—or LESS of—in your next chapter?

content:
One of the best pieces of career and business development advice is also one of the simplest: ask for what you want.

Ask for the raise. Ask for the promotion. Ask for the introduction. Ask to be considered for the opportunity, invited to the meeting, included in the pitch or given the chance to take on something bigger.

So many of us work hard and assume someone will notice, connect the dots and offer us the next opportunity. Sometimes that happens. Often, we need to speak up and make our goals known.

I know asking can feel uncomfortable, especially when the answer might be no. 

But a no leaves you exactly where you were before you asked. 

A yes could change your career, your business or your life. And sometimes the conversation that follows opens a door you hadn’t even considered.

People can’t support goals they don’t know you have. They can’t make an introduction if they don’t know you want one. They can’t consider you for an opportunity if you’ve never expressed interest.

Be clear about what you want and give people the chance to say yes. What’s something you’ve been meaning to ask for?

content:
One of the most unhelpful myths we tell young people is that they should know what they want to do with their lives by the time they leave school or university.

Some do.
Most don’t.
And that’s perfectly normal.

Careers are rarely as linear as they look on LinkedIn.

You try things. You learn. You change direction. You discover strengths you didn’t know you had and interests you couldn’t possibly have predicted at 18 or 21.

My advice?

Pay attention.

Pay attention to the work you enjoy.

Pay attention to what you’re naturally good at.

Pay attention to what other people consistently value in you.

Then keep looking for ways to do more of those things and, ideally, get paid for them.

You don’t need your entire career mapped out.

You need enough self-awareness to recognise the clues.

Your startup doesn’t need more advice.

It needs a point of view.

Founders can spend months collecting frameworks, opinions and “best practices” until every decision sounds reasonable, and none of them feel owned.

A stronger approach:

Choose what you believe about your customer, your category and how you want to win.

Then let that belief shape:

• What you build
• Who you say no to
• How you sell
• What you measure
• Which opportunities you ignore

Your point of view will not be right forever. But without one, the loudest voice in the room becomes your strategy.

If you can’t find a job in new country, come up with a startup idea

Almost every city has organizations that support startups: business incubators, accelerators, innovation hubs, startup communities, and similar programs.

Many of them run free programs that last for a few months and are open to people who are still at the idea stage. Some are online, some offline.

 There you can:
→ meet people who know the local market
→ understand how business works in your new country
→ build a professional network
→ potentially find your first clients
→ meet a co-founder for your idea
→ discover someone else’s project and join their team
→ improve your language skills

Basically, it can be several months of free, real-world practice in your new market.

So if you’re currently between jobs and have some time on your hands, this could be a pretty useful way to spend it.

"The first year in startup life is the EASIEST."

Most founders say the first year is the hardest.
But serial founder Lennard Kooy from Lleverage disagrees.

"Year one is the honeymoon phase".
Everyone is excited.
You're running on adrenaline.

Then reality kicks in.
You raise money, hire people, expectations go up.
➤ Investors want results.
➤ Employees want answers.
➤ Customers want the product to actually work.

Suddenly you’re not “building a startup.”
You’re responsible for a company.

That’s the phase nobody romanticizes.
Building can be incredibly rewarding.
But it’s also brutally hard, psychologically demanding and definitely not for everyone.

Maybe the real founder test isn’t whether you can start.
It’s whether you still want to push through when the excitement wears off.

The first sales hire at a startup is the most consequential one.

Most founders get it wrong by hiring too senior, too fast — a polished enterprise rep who's never had to build their own pipeline.

What actually works: the rep who was #1 or #2 at a company in your space, one stage earlier. Someone who figured out the messaging themselves, ran their own outbound, and closed without a full support team behind them.

Three things to test for:
→ Can they sell in ambiguity? Give them your real ICP, your real objection.
→ Do they understand your specific buyer — not a generic pitch?
→ Are they willing to do the grind before the glory? Early-stage AEs prospect, demo, close, and onboard. All of it.

The best founding AEs aren't actively looking. Finding them takes reach.

Startups learn quickly that the idea in the founder's head is not the same thing as a problem a customer will pay to solve.

That lesson belongs in school long before a student starts a company.

Customer discovery teaches a powerful set of habits:
- curiosity before certainty;
- listening without leading the witness;
- separating a need from a preferred solution;
- finding patterns without erasing outliers; and
- changing direction when evidence disagrees with your favorite idea.

Those are startup skills. They are also research skills, collaboration skills, and basic intellectual humility.

My favorite student entrepreneurship projects do not begin with "What business should we start?" They begin with "Who experiences a problem we should understand better?"

Teach the interview before the pitch deck.

𝗩𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗲𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗗𝗼𝘂𝗴 𝗟𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲: 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗧𝗼 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗔 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆

Don’t start a company because being a founder sounds exciting.

Start because you have a burning need to solve something.

Doug Leone’s point is simple: entrepreneurship is too difficult to pursue casually.

Key Takeaways:

1️⃣ Start with obsession
The problem should matter enough that you cannot stop thinking about it.

2️⃣ Do not manufacture a startup idea
The strongest companies often begin with a problem the founder deeply understands.

3️⃣ You need staying power
When things inevitably get hard, genuine conviction is what keeps you going.

Bottom line?

Don’t start a company because you want to be an entrepreneur.

Start because you feel you have to build it.

👉Enough sales to understand objections.

You don't need to master everything.

But you do need to become comfortable operating outside your comfort zone.

Your ability to learn may become your biggest competitive advantage.

Especially in environments where yesterday's playbook no longer works.

content:
Dear Founder,

We know how your story begins.
“I had an idea.”

Then came the pitch deck.The first prototype.
The first user.The first yes.
Maybe there was funding.
Maybe there was a little hype.
Maybe, for a while, everything looked like it was going exactly as planned. And then… silence.
The website stopped updating.
The Instagram went quiet.
The announcements stopped coming.

And one day, someone asked:
“Whatever happened to them?”
That question is where we begin.
Because a startup doesn’t disappear in a single day.
There are usually dozens of little moments before the final one.

A number that didn’t look right.
A customer who didn’t return.
A team member who left.
A market that moved.
A decision that bought time but cost momentum.
None of these moments necessarily look like the end when they happen.

That’s the interesting part.
So we’re going back.

Not to rewrite the story.

content:
I've been thinking about what the role of a founder really means.
I don't believe a founder is the person who does everything.
A founder is the person who sets the direction.
He carries the vision, communicates it clearly, and brings the right people together to turn that vision into reality.
He may not be the best person to develop the product, lead sales, manage HR, or handle every operational detail. But he should know how to identify the right people for the right roles—and give them the trust, clarity, and ownership to do their best work.
At the same time, a founder cannot simply delegate and step away.
Every major decision carries accountability—to the customers who trust the company, to the people who have chosen to build it, and to the investors who have placed their trust in the vision.
I believe a founder should constantly ask:
Are we moving in the right direction?
Are we creating real value for our customers?
Are we doing right by our people?
Are we building something worth believing in?
And perhaps most importantly, a founder should have a strong desire to never let the team down.
Failure will happen. Wrong decisions will happen. Plans will break.
But when things fall apart, that's when the founder's character matters most.
The ability to stand back up, learn quickly, bring the team together, and return with even greater energy to fix what went wrong.
To me, being a founder isn't about having all the answers.
It's about having the vision to know where to go, the judgement to choose the right people, the courage to make difficult decisions, and the resilience to keep moving when the path becomes difficult.
Build the vision.
Build the team.
Take the responsibility.
Keep moving forward.

content:
If everything is urgent, the founder becomes the bottleneck
  
Most founders do not struggle because they cannot make decisions.  They struggle because too many decisions land on their desk every day.
  
A client needs an answer. A team member needs direction. A proposal needs review. A contractor wants to know what takes priority. A delivery issue needs attention.
  
Each request may be reasonable. But when there is no clear operating framework, the founder becomes the person who decides what happens next.
  
That creates a business where the loudest request gets attention first, while important strategic work gets pushed to “when things calm down.”
  
A stronger operation clarifies priorities, ownership, and escalation points. It gives the team a way to move work forward without waiting for the founder to weigh in on every detail.
  
Your attention is too valuable to spend all day resolving decisions that a better system could handle.

One of the biggest traps for a founder is being good at solving problems.

At the beginning, it helps.

Something goes wrong, you fix it.

A customer complains, you handle it.

There is an operational problem, you step in.

Someone doesn’t know what to do, you make the decision.

And because you’re usually faster, it feels efficient.

But over time, something happens.

Everyone starts coming to you.

And eventually, you become the system.

That’s not scale.

If every decision needs the founder, you haven’t really built an organization yet.

You’ve built yourself a very demanding job.

I’m still working on this myself.

The goal isn’t to become better at solving every problem.

It’s to build people, systems and accountability so fewer problems need me in the first place.

A business becomes more valuable when the founder becomes less necessary.

Every approval.

Every piece of content.

Every small problem.

Then documenting it.

Delegating it.

Building systems around it.

And eventually removing yourself from it.

The goal isn’t to become unnecessary.

The goal is to make your highest-value contribution possible.
