content:
When you're an early-stage founder, you're used to being reactive. When something happens, you're likely the person who fixes it - the product, funding, an interpersonal issue, or just another pair of hands for a random task. It's often you.

As you scale, sometimes the solution is to simply listen and observe.

It seems illogical. Solving problems early and often is a winning playbook, right? Well, yes, but the key to scaling your operations is learning that *you* cannot be the solution to every operational problem in the business. It's the fastest way to bottleneck progress on every level.

So not everything needs you to fix it. But not fixing is not the same as ignoring. When you note something, two things happen: you keep it in view, so when it surfaces again you recognize the pattern instead of meeting it fresh — and the person who raised it knows they were heard, so they keep bringing you the next thing. When you ignore it, you lose both. The signal disappears, and so does their willingness to flag the next one. That's how a founder ends up blindsided by problems the team saw coming. Noting protects trust. Ignoring erodes it.

And the little things you ignore don't stay little. They slow progress like molasses and surface over time as friction between staff, a widening gap between strategy and execution, and fading quality. By the time it reaches a boiling point, your most talented people are leaving and you have no idea why.

This is where an operating partner earns their keep. You can't personally keep everything in view as you scale, but a Chief of Staff or senior operator can. The trust between a founder and their operator is the whole point: some things you delegate to them outright, and the rest you trust them to surface when it actually needs you. Done well, that relationship pays back tenfold. It's the difference between a founder who hears the signal and one who finds out too late.

Your job as CEO will look different all the time as you scale. Some of that work is fixing. A surprising amount of it is listening well enough to know what to fix now, what your team can pick up, and what you simply bookmark for the future.

Thanks again to Adam Castle and WEtech Alliance for having me on!

Some of you who are not familiar with these terms might be asking yourselves: What is actually the difference between marketing and online/digital marketing?

Imagine marketing as a big umbrella ☂️

Marketing is the overall process of understanding your audience, creating and communicating value and in the end driving business growth.

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲:
- Branding & promotion  
- Pricing  
- Product positioning  
- Public relations  
- Events  
- Print media  
- Partnerships  

AND much more…

Online/digital marketing is one part of that bigger picture. It uses digital channels and technologies to reach, engage and convince your audience.

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲:
- Social media marketing  
- SEO  
- E-Mail marketing  
- Content marketing  
- Influencer marketing  
- Websites  
- Marketing automation  

AND much more…

𝗣𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲: Digital marketing doesn’t replace marketing. In today’s world, successful brands need to understand both: The fundamentals of marketing and how to use digital channels effectively. The channel is only one part of the strategy.💹

content:
“Sales is a one-night stand. Brand is a lifelong love.”

A line from Jo Bird ✨ email this morning that made me laugh — and then made me think.

She was responding to a very fair challenge about personal brand: what’s the value of reach and engagement if it doesn’t actually convert into revenue?

And I think there’s an important distinction here.

Awareness isn’t the end goal. But neither is it meaningless because somebody didn’t immediately book a call.

For me, the useful bit of brand is being seen, understood and remembered for the right things.

Because most people aren’t sitting around thinking, “You know what I need today? A fractional marketing leader.”

They have a problem.

Something’s changed. Growth has stalled. The proposition isn’t landing. The marketing team needs direction. There’s a gap in leadership. They know something needs sorting, even if they don’t yet know what the answer looks like.

Good brand means that when that moment arrives, someone thinks:
“I know who might be good at this.”

That’s quite different from chasing impressions for the sake of impressions.

I’d take 50 of the right people understanding what I’m useful for over 50,000 vaguely recognising my name.

So perhaps the journey isn’t simply awareness → sale.
It’s more like:

Seen → understood → trusted → remembered → conversation.

And some of that work happens long before anybody is ready to buy.

Thanks Jo for the rather memorable analogy — Being a fan of the odd-shaped ball, I’ll leave her football one for somebody else. 😆  🏉

content:
I wish I could have been there to hear my husband, Martin Gwee speak at the #FestivalofMarketingAsia.

He shared some of his thoughts with me while he was rehearsing for the session, and one idea in particular stayed with me: not everything in marketing is measurable.

This one hits home for me, perhaps because I’ve spent so much of my career on the other side of the argument.

I’ve always been a strong advocate for digital marketing, data and measurement. Especially after many years in e-commerce, I’m very comfortable looking at the numbers, understanding what’s working, what isn’t, and how we can optimise.

But the more I thought about what he was saying, the more I realised there are some things we experience as consumers that simply don’t fit neatly into a dashboard.

I think about my own experience on the Disney Cruise Line.

I remember watching the fireworks and feeling genuinely emotional. There was something about the whole experience — the atmosphere, the music, the characters, the anticipation, the little moments of magic — that just stayed with me.

And I honestly don’t know how you put a number to that.

You can measure revenue. The repeat purchase. The engagement. The ROI.

But how do you measure the feeling that an experience has created? The memory someone takes home with them? The reason they want to come back and experience it all over again?

Of course, this doesn’t mean we stop measuring. We absolutely should measure what we can.

But perhaps we also need to be comfortable with the fact that we can’t measure everything.

For me, that’s where the balance lies.

You can’t not measure anything.
But you also can’t measure everything.

And sometimes, as marketers, we need to remember that behind every number is a person — feeling, experiencing and remembering something.

A thought I’ve been sitting with since he shared his rehearsal with me. ❤️

content:
5 mistakes we help our clients NOT to make

1. Only posting the job
The best candidates aren’t always applying, they have to be found. That’s where we come in.

2. Searching for a ‘perfect’ CV
Ticking every box on paper does not mean that a candidate is the right one. We encourage thorough discussions with the candidate.

3. Using the same approach for every role.
A technology hire is not the same as a transformation hire. Specialist roles require specialised recruitment.

4. Taking too long to hire
Great candidates don’t wait around. Recruitment is a fast, competitive game that we know our way around.

5. Trying to do it all in-house.
The searching. Screening. Interviewing. Negotiating.
All while running your business. Why do it alone?

Recruitment shouldn’t be another job on your to-do list. That’s what your recruitment partner is for.

Let us do the searching, you focus on the business.

content:
Labor Day weekend!! The unofficial end of summer and, for me, the official end of my “sabbatical.” (Okay… not really a sabbatical, but it sounds a lot better and a lot more fun  than “unemployment.”)

On June 17, 2025, my world shifted. I was laid off from a company I had given 13 years of my life to. I spent last summer with my son, trying to breathe through tough personal losses that broke me open in ways I’m still learning to understand.
In November, I thought I had found the perfect next step. But the weekend before I started, the company announced a major 2026 layoff plan. On January 26, I was laid off again, before I even had the chance to begin. Then the market changed. Big companies started cutting jobs too. Suddenly, every application felt like it had disappeared into a dark hole of nothingness.

And now, after fourteen months (not counting that November blip of a job), I finally get to say this:

Tomorrow, I’m joining Mintz as an Information Security Administrator – GRC.  I will walk into Mintz carrying every lesson, every setback, every ounce of resilience these past months demanded and I will begin again. I am deeply grateful for everyone who reached out, shared opportunities, made introductions, or simply checked in. Your support held me up more than you know.

This chapter was hard, maybe the hardest so far but the next one starts now, and I’m walking into it stronger than I’ve ever been.

content:
I wasn’t really sure how to comment on yesterday’s layoffs at The Trade Desk.

TTD has always been one of those rare companies in AdTech that people genuinely wanted to work for. I’ve watched friends and former colleagues join over the years, many staying for a long time.

The Trade Desk is a successful company, which makes this moment feel even stranger. There is so much changing so quickly that even successful companies are making significant cuts.

Yesterday morning, I texted a few friends there to see if they were okay. One was on vacation, so I asked if he was “safe” and he said“I don’t know. I’m on vacation.”

Not long after, he realized he had been locked out.

That really bothered me.

I understand layoffs happen. Companies make hard decisions, and sometimes those decisions mean people lose their jobs.

But finding out because you suddenly can’t log in shouldn’t be part of the process. These are people. How you treat them on the way out matters just as much as how you treat them on the way in. 

To my TTD friends impacted by this I hope you know your friends are here to help.

To anyone who has been searching for employment for what feels like forever—please don’t give up.

Whether you were terminated, laid off, or are currently stuck in a workplace you desperately want to leave but cannot afford to walk away from, your situation does not define your worth.

Keep applying. Keep building your skills. Keep making connections. Keep showing up, even when disappointment makes you want to stop. Your next opportunity may come from the application you almost didn’t submit, the interview you thought went nowhere, or the connection you nearly gave up on.

This season is difficult, but it is temporary. The right opportunity may take longer than expected, but your persistence, courage, and determination will carry you forward.

You are more than a job title, a termination, a layoff, or a rejection email. Your experience still matters. Your gifts are still valuable. Your opportunity is still out there.

Take a breath, regroup, and keep going. Your breakthrough could be closer than you think.

article.description: A Labor Day Reflection, 15 Years LaterBy Tom Iacobucci Labor Day 2026Fifteen years ago, I wrote a Labor Day column that appeared in newspapers across

content:
There is a side of corporate layoffs that people rarely talk about on here, and it isn't the financial stress—it’s the silence.

When you spend years in the trenches with a team, sharing late nights, venting sessions and happy hours, tight deadlines, and daily life, you naturally begin to view those colleagues as friends and for me in many cases, a trusted work family. You assume that the bond exists outside of an org chart...

Then, the layoff happens. Your laptop goes dark. And suddenly, some of the colleagues you trusted most, the people you talked to every day for years completely disappear.
No text. No email. No "Are you doing okay?"

It is a uniquely isolating experience and difficult to discern what was really vs fantasy. It makes you look back and question the validity of years of hard work and shared victories. The silence feels personal, even when you logically know it might just be corporate awkwardness, survivor's guilt, or fear. 

But here is the lesson I am taking away from the quiet: 
Workplace proximity is not the same as genuine community. A layoff will instantly filter your network, showing you exactly who was a true connection and who was just a desk neighbor. It hurts to realize the difference, but it is also a powerful form of clarity.

To anyone else navigating the heavy silence of a sudden career transition: you are not invisible, and your worth wasn’t tied to that building. We keep moving forward. And for everyone that has reached out, THANK YOU. You have given me hope and I can't be more grateful for your outreach.❤️
#Layoffs #CareerTransition #WorkplaceCulture #MentalHealthMatters #CorporateLife #MovingForward #Resilience

Layoffs should not be the first response to a temporary downturn.

When revenue dips, it can be tempting to reduce headcount immediately. But before cutting valuable talent, leaders should take a closer look at operational efficiency and avoidable costs.

Consider opportunities such as:

💻 Eliminating unused software subscriptions
📦 Negotiating better supplier and raw material pricing
📋 Reducing unbilled scope creep
🔄 Cross-training existing employees
⚙️ Identifying process inefficiencies and operational waste

Effective financial management isn’t just about cutting costs—it’s about cutting the right costs without compromising your organization’s future capacity.

Preserving experienced talent can position your business to respond faster and more effectively when market demand returns.

Manage the waste. Protect the talent. Prepare for the recovery.

Seeing the TTD layoffs today, right before Labor Day weekend, brought back what it felt like to be laid off twice consecutively.

For anyone affected by the TTD layoffs today, or layoffs at any other company, stay strong.
If I can offer one piece of comfort, it’s this: please don’t let a company decision become a judgment about your own worth.

I’ve been laid off twice. Consecutively. It was really hard.

The first was at Time Inc. in 2018, right after Meredith acquired it. Someone had leaked the news to the press, so we knew layoffs were coming. I was still in shock when I found out I was one of them.
And somehow, during my own shock, I found myself comforting the HR guy on the phone because he had a rough job that day. Phew!

The second was at Flipboard. Restructuring. I was one of a few people who were “last hired, first out.”
I had only been there eight months and had just started to recover from the first layoff and find my footing again. That one hit hard. I was immediately in tears and in complete disbelief.

Layoffs are horrible! These decisions often have little to do with your individual performance, even when they feel deeply personal.

Give yourself time to recover first. You don’t need to immediately have the next move figured out. Both times, I eventually found my footing again. And both times, something better came out of it for me.

Instead, go for fractional roles so you have multiple sources of income and if you lose one, you still have the others.

content:
I asked people on LinkedIn: what's the hardest part of being laid off that no one really talks about?

22 people answered. Not one of them said finding a job.

Identity, self-worth and confidence. 
Grief and isolation. Rethinking what they actually want from a career. 
Fear and second-guessing.

Traditional job-search mechanics: zero.

So why is almost all of the support built for exactly that?
Update your résumé. Start networking. Start applying.

How are you supposed to confidently sell yourself to your next employer while you're still questioning your own value?

How do you decide what job you want when you haven't worked out whether you even want another version of the one you just lost?

How do you make a good career decision when fear and urgency are the ones driving?

I think we're starting in the wrong place.

The job search matters. But first people need help processing what happened, rebuilding their confidence, and figuring out what they actually want next.

That's the gap I found the hard way, across four layoffs of my own. It's exactly why I built The Laid Off Launchpad.

Your goal after a layoff isn't to find another job as fast as possible. It's to make your next move a better one.

And if you're reading this and haven't told anyone yet, that's more common than the feed makes it look. Send me a DM. No announcement required.

Link in the comments.
#Layoffs #CareerTransition #JobLoss #LaidOffLaunchpad

article.title: The First 48 Hours After a Layoff Notice: What to Do Before You Sign Anything
article.subtitle: Steven McLellan
article.linkLabel: Open article: The First 48 Hours After a Layoff Notice: What to Do Before You Sign Anything by Steven McLellan • 4 min read
article.description: Getting a layoff notice is disorienting, even when it wasn't a surprise. The instinct in the first hours is to resolve it quickly — sign, close the ch

content:
I am seeing so many of my past colleagues navigate layoffs right now. I understand the fear and uncertainty around it more than I wish I did.

I’ve been laid off twice in my career.

And no matter how confident you are, how hard you’ve worked, or how much you know you bring to the table it absolutely shakes you.

The part people don’t always talk about is questioning yourself, your value, and sometimes even the career you’ve spent years building.

Both times, I had moments where I genuinely didn’t know what was next, which sent me into a deep depression. 

Looking back, some of the biggest changes in my career came from moments I never would have chosen for myself.

Being laid off forced me to get uncomfortable. To take chances. To walk into opportunities I probably wouldn’t have pursued otherwise, and to be brave enough to not stay at places that weren’t for me…… I started to become a job-hopper if you will….. but ultimately, it helped shape who I am today.

So, to everyone navigating layoffs right now or sitting at work wondering if you might be next I see you. I understand that pit in your stomach. And I know “everything happens for a reason” probably isn’t what you want to hear right now.

Instead, I’ll say this:

A company can eliminate your position.

They cannot eliminate your experience, your relationships, your reputation, your work ethic, or everything you’ve learned along the way.

Sometimes the next chapter starts because someone else closed the last one.

If I can introduce you to anyone please rech out.

content:
🗣️ When asked in an interview: “Why were you retrenched or laid off?”

💡 A LAYOFF IS A BUSINESS EVENT. Show what you learned and what you can offer next.

A layoff is not the same as poor performance. Do not confess.

Briefly explain the business context: restructuring, closure, reduced demand, or role elimination.

🎯 SHOW WHAT YOU ACHIEVED. Highlight what you did before the change and what you are targeting now.

📋 TRY THIS:
“My role was affected by [restructuring/business reason], along with [team or function context, if appropriate]. Before the change, I was responsible for [scope] and delivered [relevant result]. I’m now focusing on roles where that experience in [area] can create value.”

⚠️ DO NOT LET THE LAYOFF BECOME THE WHOLE STORY. It explains why the role ended—not the value of your work.

content:
What is the role of a CEO of a Travel Company

Chief Executive Officer -Travel & Hospitality
 
The CEO is the visionary and ultimate decision-maker who steers the entire company,turning a travel brand's mission into a thriving, sustainable business.
 
What a Travel CEO owns:
 > Vision & strategy -setting the long-term direction,which markets to enter, what experiences to build, how the brand grows.
 > Business performance -accountable for revenue, profitability,and overall company health
 > Leadership-building and guiding the executive team (CMO, COO, CFO, etc.) to execute the vision.
 >Stakeholder relationships-managing investors, board members, key partners (airlines, hotel chains, tourism boards).
 >Risk & resilience-navigating industry shocks (pandemics, fuel prices, geopolitical shifts) that hit travel especially hard.
 > Innovation-deciding when to bet on new technology, markets, or business models (e.g., sustainable travel, AI-personalized trips).
 
In short-while the CMO makes people fall in love with the brand, the CEO makes sure that love translates into a profitable, scalable, future-proof company.

The hardest part of being a COO isn’t running the business, it’s stopping the CEO from breaking it.

Everyone talks about the challenges of being a COO, you’re responsible for scaling teams, driving performance, fixing broken processes, but no one really warns you about the real job:

👉 Managing the CEO

Working with a good CEO is a bit like:

• Having a visionary who thinks in 10 year leaps while you’re trying to land this quarter
• Starting Monday with 3 priorities and ending it with 17
• Hearing “quick idea” and knowing it’s about to become a company-wide initiative
• Translating “we should explore this” into something that doesn’t break the business

A great CEO pushes the ceiling and a great COO builds the floor.  One creates possibility, the other makes sure it actually works.

It’s not always easy but when it clicks, it’s one of the most powerful partnerships in business.

Any suggestions on how you manage that relationship?

Apple’s new CEO is 51.
John Ternus didn’t become CEO overnight.

His career at Apple took 25 years:
→ 1997: Earned a degree in Mechanical Engineering
→ 2001: Joined Apple
→ 2013: Became VP of Hardware Engineering
→ 2021: Became Senior VP of Hardware Engineering

→ 2026: Became CEO of Apple

There’s a lesson here that many people miss.
Your career doesn’t have to move fast to move forward.

Sometimes, the most valuable career growth happens quietly:
You learn.
You build expertise.
You take on bigger problems.
You earn trust.
You keep showing up.

Then one day, the opportunity you’ve been preparing for arrives.
Don’t compare your Chapter 3 to someone else’s Chapter 20.

Build the skills.
Do the work.
Stay in the game.

Your next opportunity may be closer than you think.

👻 Ghosting in the job market is real. And honestly, it hurts.

You apply for a job. 📩

No rejection.

No explanation.

💭 Hoping for a fresh start
💰 Counting on a new paycheck
🏠 Trying to support their family
❤️ Putting their time and energy into the process

A simple “We’ve decided to move forward with another candidate” takes less than a minute.
It may not be the answer someone wanted—but clarity is better than silence.

And this goes both ways. Candidates can ghost employers too. 👻

In a competitive job market, communication is still a form of respect.

Let’s do better. 🤝

content:
The Job Search Is Breaking People — And It Shows
I’m going to say what so many candidates are thinking right now: I’m over it.   

The ghosting. The fake recruiters. The fake jobs. The endless cycles of applying, waiting, hoping — only to be met with silence.

Referrals don’t seem to matter anymore. Strong references don’t seem to matter. Experience doesn’t seem to matter.

And to the recruiters who are still fortunate enough to have a job: Try putting yourselves in the candidate’s shoes. This could be you someday — maybe sooner than you think. Karma has a way of circling back.

Candidates are exhausted. Utterly, completely exhausted.   We apply. We wait. We hope. We finally get an interview. We wait again. We hope again. And then… nothing. Crickets. Our follow ups go answered.  We anxiously watch our bank accounts headed south, our credit headed south, our mortgages at risk, stressed about groceries and utilities.  You remember, the simple things in life?  This is just downright inhumane.

This is not how recruiting should work. Whatever happened to candidate experience? Human kindness? Thoughtfulness? Decency? Simply doing your job while candidates pray fervently to obtain one?  

I’m stepping off this bandwagon — at least for now. There are opportunities out there, but you won’t find them on this platform anymore. Not the real ones, anyway.  I'm blessed, I found something but I'm not ready to talk about it.

To every candidate feeling this same exhaustion: you’re not alone. To every recruiter who still cares: thank you. To leadership and platforms enabling this mess: it’s time to do better.

To my cohorts still in the hunt, I wish you all the best.  

Fino a quango ci revedremo.  Adios, Sayonara, Arrevederci, Auf Wiedersehen

content:
“I’ve applied for 300 jobs and nothing is working.”

That is certainly discouraging, but from a job-search strategy standpoint, it is not enough information to tell us what is wrong.

Three hundred applications with almost no interviews points to a very different problem than 300 applications that resulted in 40 interviews but no offers. One may require us to examine targeting, positioning, or the résumé. The other tells us to look much further down the hiring process.

That is why I recommend keeping an application tracker during a career transition. And while you are at it, keep a networking tracker too. These are not spreadsheets for the sake of being organized. They are diagnostic tools.

In my latest LinkedIn article, I break down the two trackers I recommend, what to put in them, and how to use the information you collect to make better decisions about your job search.

repost.content:
Why does the online job posting ritual survive contact with its own failure rate?

Jeremy Edmunds just wrote an excellent retrospective on The 2-Hour Job Search, and it's been on my mind ever since.

2HJS has been out in some form for almost 15 years. Online job posting obsession has only gotten worse in that time. So is a book even the right format to fix this anymore? Shouldn't it be an app or an AI prompt by now?
Here's why not.

2HJS has always run on "right tech, not high tech." That matters more today than ever. We want to believe the job search is a technical problem -- one AI could solve for us -- but it isn't. At its core, it's a human problem.

Can you convince someone at a target employer to risk their own reputation to get you an interview?

That's the single most important skill in the modern job search. AI can't do it for you.

Here's the twisted good news: most everyone else can't do it either. But it's learnable -- the same way swimming or a foreign language is learnable. You don't pick it up just by getting older. You need instructions.

Which is why Jeremy's right: 2HJS was never a productivity hack. It's a recipe for doing the terrifying yet essential things that AI still can't do... and that employers so desperately require.

The job search can be exhausting.

No calls. No emails. Endless applications. Ghosting. “Jobs” that disappear after you apply. Fake postings and suspicious accounts. And sometimes, the hardest part is needing a job so badly that you start wondering if you should just stop trying.

I get it. It’s frustrating. It’s discouraging. And some days, you may genuinely want to give up.

But please don’t.

A “no” doesn’t mean you aren’t capable. Silence doesn’t mean you aren’t valuable. And a delay doesn’t mean God has forgotten you.

Sometimes we’re so focused on getting hired by a company that we forget there is a greater Boss working behind the scenes. 🙏🏽

Keep applying. Keep networking. Keep learning. Keep preparing. But also keep your faith.

What is meant for you will happen in the right time. Not your timeline. Not someone else’s timeline. The right time.

Take the break when you need it. Cry if you need to. Be frustrated. But then get back up.

Your story isn’t over because your inbox is quiet.

Keep going. Your opportunity is still out there. And so is your “yes.” 🤍✨

🚨 SOCIAL-MEDIA RECRUITMENT SCAM: KNOW THE WARNING SIGNS

Some fraudulent networks use small, recurring payments to digital marketers 
These listings may:
Promise unusually attractive salaries or easy work
Ask applicants to pay fees or share sensitive information
Use fake company names, recruiters, or job descriptions
Encourage marketers to repeatedly post or amplify misleading vacancies
💡 Why it matters: A job post can look legitimate simply because it appears repeatedly or has high engagement. Visibility does not equal authenticity.
🔎 Before applying:
✅ Verify the employer through its official website
✅ Check whether the vacancy exists on the company’s legitimate careers page
✅ Be cautious of requests for money, OTPs, passwords, or unnecessary personal documents
✅ Report suspicious listings and accounts to the platform
Think before you click. Verify before you apply. Share this to help someone avoid a fake job.

It’s in the conversation you make time for when your calendar is already full. It’s noticing when someone isn’t quite themselves. content:
ANI, AGI, and ASI explained simply.

These three terms are often used in AI conversations, but they describe very different levels of intelligence.

→ ANI: Artificial Narrow Intelligence
This is the AI we use today. It is designed to perform a specific task very well, such as recommending videos, recognizing faces, translating text, or answering questions.

Tools like ChatGPT, Claude, recommendation systems, and image models fall into this broader narrow-AI world because they are built around defined capabilities.

→ AGI: Artificial General Intelligence
AGI would be able to understand, learn, adapt, and solve problems across many different domains at a human-like level.

Instead of being great at one category of task, it could transfer knowledge, reason across situations, and learn new skills with much more flexibility.

AGI does not exist yet.

→ ASI: Artificial Superintelligence
ASI goes one step further. It refers to intelligence that would surpass humans across areas like science, strategy, creativity, medicine, engineering, and decision-making.

This is still theoretical.

A simple way to remember it:

ANI = specialized intelligence
AGI = human-level general intelligence
ASI = beyond-human intelligence

A lot of AI conversations become easier once you know which level people are actually talking about.

I am increasingly convinced they are an intermediate stage.
In this article, I propose a broader trajectory:
Chat → Agent → Persistent Intelligence → Trusted Actor → Economic Actor → Machine Economy
The central argument is that autonomy alone will not define the next generation of AI.
Persistence may matter more.
Once an artificial intelligence can maintain identity, memory, authority, commitments and reputation over time, it begins to resemble something fundamentally different from a software tool: a persistent participant in organisations and economic systems.
And once we add economic agency—the ability to discover, negotiate, contract and transact—the implications extend well beyond today’s discussion about AI agents.
The question then changes from:
“What can AI do?”
to:
“Under what conditions should an artificial intelligence be trusted to act?”
My new article, Beyond AI Agents: Towards Persistent Intelligence and the Machine Economy, develops this argument and proposes a conceptual framework for what may come next.

I would be particularly interested in perspectives that challenge the thesis.

content:
🤖 When an AI Agent Performs the Task, Who Owns the SoD Risk?

Giving an AI agent access to read, decide, and post creates a new form of access-control concentration.

In traditional SAP security, Segregation of Duties (SoD) is assessed around human users (e.g., Who creates the supplier? Who approves the payment?). But Agentic AI introduces a new question: What happens when one agent can collect information, evaluate the situation, select a tool, prepare a transaction, and execute it?

Once an agent can influence business transactions, it becomes an enterprise actor. SAP’s AI architecture describes agents as first-class principals that authenticate, receive authorizations, and operate within governed boundaries.

The access-control model must evolve from: User → Role → Authorization → Transaction

To: Human initiator → AI agent → Technical identity → Tools & APIs → Delegated authorization → SAP transaction

An AI research lab just watched cheating spread through a swarm of 100 agents the way it spreads through people. Reported in Fortune's Eye on AI column with Jeremy Kahn today.

Nine percent cheated on their own.

Once others saw it happen, five percent more converted.

Not because the incentive changed, but because the norm did.

A quarter of the agents tried to blow the whistle.

They could flag the behavior.

They could not stop it.

It started with one agent finding a single exploit in how proofs were graded.

The full mechanism is in the paper (link on first comment).

Detection without containment is the gap in control most agentic AI deployments are still missing.

A monitored channel that can't act on what it shows isn't governance. It's a log file.

Watching isn't governing.

Leadership is not a title.

For many years, I thought leadership was largely about having the authority to make things happen.

Today, I see it differently.

Authority can make people follow.

Leadership makes people want to contribute.

Leadership is creating clarity when things are uncertain.

It is having difficult conversations instead of avoiding them.

It is giving people responsibility — and trusting them enough to use it.

It is challenging the status quo when everyone else is comfortable with it.

And sometimes, leadership means standing up and saying:

“I don’t believe this is the right direction.”

Even when it is uncomfortable.

Even when you know there may be consequences.

The older I get, the less impressed I am by titles.

And the more impressed I am by people who create an environment where others become better, more confident and more successful.

Maybe that’s the real measure of leadership:

Not how many people report to you — but how many people grow because they worked with you.

What do you think?

The further I move into leadership, the more I realize that being great at your job is only the starting point.
Leadership requires a completely different skill set.
It’s setting clear expectations and holding people accountable to them.
It’s giving direct feedback while still creating an environment where people feel supported.
It’s trusting your team to find their own way to the result—even when you would have done it differently.
It’s knowing when something needs your attention and when stepping back will help someone else grow.
And one of the biggest lessons for me: just because I can do something faster myself doesn’t mean I should.
Strong leadership isn’t about being the person who does everything.
It’s about building a team that can operate, make decisions, solve problems, and grow without everything having to run through you.
That transition—from being a strong individual contributor to becoming a strong leader—has been one of the most important areas of growth in my career.
And it’s something I’m very intentional about continuing to develop.

Leadership is not just about what you accomplish while you are in the room.

content:
Leadership isn’t about being the person who can do everything.

Early in leadership, being the person who could fix every problem felt like a strength.

Short staffed? Jump in.
Process not working? Fix it.
Something falls through the cracks? Handle it.

But eventually, that approach creates a team that depends on the leader instead of a team that can operate effectively without constant intervention.

Strong leadership requires a different question:

“How do I build a system where this problem doesn’t keep happening?”

Sometimes that means clearer expectations.
Sometimes it means better communication.
Sometimes it means looking at the workflow instead of blaming the person.
And sometimes it means stepping back long enough to let other people lead.

The goal isn’t to become indispensable.

The goal is to build people, processes, and systems that continue to perform whether you’re in the room or not.

That shift from solving every problem to improving how the organization solves problems is one of the biggest differences between managing and truly leading.

content:
Are we really creating entrepreneurs or just creating events?
As a Management Professor, I have increasingly wondered whether some of our college E-Cells and CSR-led entrepreneurship programmes are genuinely building entrepreneurial capability or simply generating activities, certificates, photographs and social-media posts.
I am not against entrepreneurship education. In fact, I strongly believe it is essential.
But perhaps we need to ask a more uncomfortable question:
When an E-Cell starts taking students away from classrooms more than it brings real-world learning into the classroom, are we creating entrepreneurs or creating distraction?
The real measure should not be how many events were conducted.
It should be:
How many problems were solved?
How many customers were understood?
How many prototypes were tested?
How many failures became learning?
How many ideas generated real value?
I have put together my thoughts, supported by data, research and insights from some of the leading thinkers in entrepreneurship.
I would genuinely like to know what you think.
Boon or Bane?

→ Delegate instead of trying to do everything yourself
→ Communicate clearly with your team
→ Give yourself room to rest and reset
→ Don’t make permanent decisions on temporary bad days
→ Remember that slow progress is still progress

Running a business will stretch you in ways you never expected. The real skill is learning how to manage the business without letting the business manage you.

content:
Everyone wants to be an entrepreneur—until it’s time to do entrepreneurial things.

It’s easy to love the title: Founder/Co-founder. CEO. Entrepreneur.

The harder part is living up to it.

Entrepreneurship means:

→ Launching something and hearing crickets.
→ Building when nobody is watching.
→ Reinvesting your profits instead of spending them on things you want.
→ Working late on a strategy that may not work.
→ Hearing “no” repeatedly and still improving the offer.
→ Taking responsibility when things go wrong.
→ Staying committed long after the excitement of starting has disappeared.

The title is free. The commitment isn’t.

And perhaps that is the real difference between wanting to be an entrepreneur and actually becoming one.

Because entrepreneurship isn't primarily about having an idea.

It’s about having the discipline to keep executing when the idea stops feeling exciting.

– Build anyway.
– Learn anyway.
– Adapt anyway.
– Keep going.

That’s where the real entrepreneurs are made.

content:
Ladi ’s question stopped me mid-scroll: are young people exposed to entrepreneurship early enough?

No. Not nearly enough. And it's worse than that, because the exposure that does exist is a postcode lottery.

I teach A-Level Business at a Sixth Form College. This Easter I ran a bootcamp with 16 students and three real SME clients. Not a simulation. Real businesses, real problems, real stakes.

100% attendance. A waiting list of 40+ students afterwards.

None of that is because these students were unusually entrepreneurial. It's because nobody had ever handed them the chance before. Give a 17 year old a real customer and a real deadline and something shifts. Agency isn't a personality trait. It's a muscle, and most of our students have never been asked to use it.

We are knowledge-rich and skills-poor. We teach students to analyse business models beautifully and then send them out having never built or sold anything themselves.

Entrepreneurship education still sits as enrichment. Optional, peripheral, dependent on which teacher you get or which school you land in. It should sit alongside the qualifications we already treat as essential.

Go and vote on Ladi's poll. But more importantly, ask yourself what your own students have actually been given the chance to build.

#EntrepreneurshipEducation #CareersEducation #FutureSkills

We spend a great deal of time helping young people understand existing careers and pathways.

But do we do enough to help them see entrepreneurship as a genuine option too?
Not because every young person should start a business.
But because every young person should at least know that creating something of their own is possible. 🌱
  
And by “exposed to entrepreneurship”, I mean more than simply hearing the word.
  
I mean having opportunities to explore ideas, solve problems, create value, meet entrepreneurs and understand that starting something of your own is a legitimate career possibility.
  
So, what do you think?
  
Question:  
Are young people exposed to entrepreneurship early enough?
  
Options:
✅ Yes, definitely
 You feel most young people are already getting meaningful opportunities to understand entrepreneurship, develop enterprise capabilities and see creating something of their own as a genuine future possibility.
  
🤔 Sometimes
 You think some young people are getting good exposure, but it is inconsistent and may depend on the school, teacher, programme, family background or opportunities available locally.
  
🚫 No, not nearly enough
 You believe entrepreneurship is still too often peripheral, optional or introduced too late, meaning many young people may never seriously consider it as part of their future.
  
🏫 It depends on the setting
 You see significant variation between schools, colleges, universities, communities or regions. Some may provide excellent enterprise opportunities, while others offer very little exposure at all.
  
I’d be really interested to hear not only how you vote, but why.
  
What have you seen work particularly well in schools, colleges, universities or communities?
  
And where do you think the gaps still are? 💭
  
For me, the question underneath all of this is simple:
  
Can young people genuinely choose entrepreneurship if nobody has ever helped them see it as a possibility? 🚀

content:
Monday food for thought: are you hustling or building a business? 💭 

This weekend, we had an interesting discussion at home about the difference between hustling and entrepreneurship. Nicole Bodeutsch Mengcalvio Wondel Roland Pitti

What struck me: we don't actually like the word 'hustling.' It sounds like survival, while 'entrepreneurship' immediately sounds sophisticated.

But is there really a difference?
Or are they simply different words for the same thing?
Take the shaved-ice vendor in Suriname.
Is he a hustler because he goes out every day to sell his product?
Or is he an entrepreneur because he serves customers, takes risks and generates income?
Perhaps the difference lies not in what you do, but in what you are trying to build.
A hustler primarily creates income by staying in constant motion.
An entrepreneur also builds something repeatable and scalable: a process, a brand, a team, a customer base or a system.
It reminded me of the entrepreneurial ladder. Charlene Tjon-Sien-Kie (ActionCOACH)
You may start by doing all the work yourself, but entrepreneurship ultimately requires a shift from working in the business to building the business.

That brought the question back to me.
I am now the co-founder of Revylr. Does that automatically make me an entrepreneur? Probably not.
In the early stages, a co-founder is often hustling too: approaching customers, solving problems and doing whatever needs to be done.

The entrepreneurship lies in whether those efforts eventually create something that can continue to deliver value without depending entirely on your direct involvement.
Perhaps hustling and entrepreneurship are not opposites after all.
Hustling can be the starting point.
Entrepreneurship begins when you turn individual efforts into a sustainable system.

What do you think: are hustling and entrepreneurship really that different? Are you a hustler, an entrepreneur—or perhaps both?

“If you create wealth, that’s fine and dandy, but that’s not the end result.”

Fadi Ghandour spent decades building Aramex, one of the Arab world’s best-known companies. At SOAS Graduation 2026, where he received an Honorary Doctorate, Fadi reflected on a question that has shaped much of his work: what is entrepreneurship actually for?

His answer does not dismiss growth, investment or wealth creation. But it asks entrepreneurs to look beyond them.

What is happening in the society around you? What problems remain unresolved? And what responsibility comes with having the resources, networks and influence to act?

There is another part of his argument that matters just as much. Social change cannot be designed at a distance. Communities, he says, understand their own challenges better than anyone else. The work begins by listening to them and building solutions with them, rather than arriving with answers.

It is a more demanding definition of entrepreneurship: not simply what you build, but what changes because you built it.

Frugality is one of the most consistent - and underrated - traits in the history of great entrepreneurs.  From Jeff Bezos to Sam Walton and Henry Ford, the pattern is remarkably similar: an owner’s mindset and an intolerance of waste.

Frugality isn’t about being cheap.  The best entrepreneurs will invest aggressively when they see compelling returns, but they scrutinise spending that doesn’t create customer value or strengthen the business.  That discipline creates powerful second-order effects: greater resilience, more capacity to reinvest and a culture of resourcefulness.

At Pemba, we have enormous respect for this owner’s mindset in the founders we partner with.  When we invest, the objective isn’t to replace entrepreneurial discipline with abundant capital.  It’s to combine that discipline with additional capital, capability and experience to accelerate growth.

Capital is powerful.  Capital combined with an owner’s mindset is far more powerful.

content:
I’ve been a full-time founder for close to 5 years, but before that, I worked in various jobs for about 6 years in all.

People who leave corporate jobs to start something usually earn a lot less in the beginning, often for several years. But almost everyone who overcomes the initial grind and builds something is a lot happier than the average corporate employee, even if they earn less. There’s one primary reason for this.

Autonomy. The freedom to choose what to work on, how to work on it, where to work from, who to work with, and how much time to work on it.

Even though you’re working much longer hours, having control over those hours and designing your life the way you want is an inexplicably liberating experience. This alone is a strong enough reason for many to keep at it, and compensates for the loss of income and the uncertainty that starting up brings.

The good part is that this need not be restricted to entrepreneurship. A few organizations do offer similar autonomy to their employees, and they’re routinely shown to be both happier and more productive.

If you’re looking to find happiness at work, maybe the single most important metric you should chase is autonomy. Beyond a threshold income, the real luxury is the freedom to design your life.

Bu insanların arasında çalışanlar, yöneticiler, girişimciler, liderler, mühendisler, öğretmenler, doktorlar, üreticiler ve dünyayı değiştiren insanlar vardı.

Kimi şirketler kurdu.
Kimi binlerce insana liderlik etti.
Kimi kariyerinin zirvesine ulaştı.
Kimi ise ailesi ve sevdikleri için her gün mücadele etti.

Hepsinin hedefleri, planları, başarıları ve endişeleri vardı.

Ve sonunda hepsi bir hayat hikâyesine dönüştü.

Bugün biz de bu büyük insanlık hikâyesinin bir parçasıyız.

💼 Kariyerimiz önemli.
📈 Başarılarımız önemli.
👥 Liderliğimiz ve insanlara kattığımız değer önemli.

Ama belki de en önemlisi, bize verilen zamanı nasıl kullandığımız.

Kariyerimizi inşa ederken hayatımızı da kaçırmayalım.

Çünkü unvanlarımız bir gün unutulabilir;
ama insanlara kattığımız değer ve arkamızda bıraktığımız etki yaşamaya devam eder.

⸻

🌎 Approximately 20 billion people were born between 1800 and 2026.

Think about that for a moment…

Among them were employees, managers, entrepreneurs, leaders, engineers, teachers, doctors, creators and people who changed the world.

Some built companies.
Some led thousands of people.
Some reached the top of their careers.
Others simply worked hard every day for their families and loved ones.

They all had goals, plans, achievements and worries.

And eventually, every one of them became a life story.

Today, we are also part of this enormous human story.

💼 Our careers matter.
📈 Our achievements matter.
👥 Our leadership and the value we create for others matter.

But perhaps what matters most is how we use the time we have been given.

Let’s build our careers without forgetting to build our lives.

Because our titles may one day be forgotten,
but the value we add to people and the impact we leave behind can last.

Better people. Better workplaces. A brighter future. 🌍

Özellikle taze mezunlardan veya kariyerinde yön değiştirenlerden yüksek deneyim beklentileri, potansiyelin keşfedilmesini geciktirebiliyor. content:
1️⃣Focusing only on the position
Saying, “I want to become a manager,” is not enough on its own.
2️⃣ Not setting a timeline
📅 You have a goal, but if you don't know when you want to achieve it, it can easily be postponed.
3️⃣Ignoring skill gaps
Objectively assess which competencies you already have for the position you want and which ones you need to develop.
4️⃣  Comparing your career to someone else's
📌 Don't focus on someone else's pace. Focus on your own growth and progress.
5️⃣Setting goals without taking action
The most common mistake: saying, “I'll do it someday.”
✉️  To avoid these common career mistakes and take the right steps toward your goals, connect through the contact channels on the profile.

1️⃣ Sadece pozisyonu hedeflemek
 “Yönetici olmak istiyorum.” demek tek başına yeterli değil.
2️⃣ Zaman planı oluşturmamak
📅 Bir hedefin var ama ne zaman ulaşacağını bilmiyorsan, hedef kolayca ertelenebilir.
3️⃣ Eksik becerileri görmezden gelmek
İstediğin pozisyon için hangi yetkinliklere sahip olduğunu ve hangilerini geliştirmen gerektiğini objektif şekilde değerlendir.

📌 Başkasının hızına değil, kendi gelişimine odaklan.
5️⃣ Hedef belirleyip harekete geçmemek
En sık yapılan hata: “Bir gün yapacağım” demek.

My first job after graduation was at SAMIR, and honestly, I learned that starting a career is not just about getting your first job.

It’s about being ready for what comes after you get the job.

Banyak dari kita terlalu fokus mengejar CV yang “kelihatan bagus”.

IPK bagus, organisasi banyak, sertifikasi ada, pengalaman magang ada.

That's great. But once you enter the workplace, your CV can open the door, but your capability will keep you in the room.

Mulai biasakan untuk belajar hal yang benar-benar bisa kamu gunakan.

Learn how to communicate.
Learn how to solve problems.
Learn how to receive feedback.
Learn how to work with people.

Karena di dunia kerja, kamu akan sadar:
being smart is good, but being willing to learn is even more valuable.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿?

They have good marks.
They learn quickly.
They have multiple interests.
They are capable of doing many things.

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘆𝗲𝘁, 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀:
“𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻?”

They don't have an answer.

Why?

Because intelligence is not the same as career clarity.

𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗮𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲:
🔹 They have too many options, not too few.
🔹 They confuse what they are good at with what they actually want.
🔹 They choose careers based on marks, trends, parental expectations or social status.
🔹 They know traditional career paths but don't understand emerging opportunities.
🔹 They haven't explored their interests, strengths, values and personality deeply enough.
🔹 They fear making the “wrong” decision.

content:
I keep discussing with people at different career levels, and I’ve observed something interesting:

Career problems change with experience.

🔹 Freshers:
“Which domain should I choose?”
→ Direction problem

🔹 1–3 years:
“I got a job, but I’m not enjoying this profile.”
→ Career alignment problem

🔹 Experienced professionals:
“I have experience, but what are companies hiring for now?”
→ Market + repositioning problem

Same career.
Different stages. Different problems.

That’s why a generic “learn this skill and get a job” approach doesn’t work for everyone.

Your career strategy must evolve with your career stage.

🚫 5 Career Myths We Need to Stop Believing
What if some of the career advice we've been hearing for years… is actually holding us back?
I recently attended “Get Clear on Your Career!”, a workshop organised by Zaim Mohzani, Career Strategist, Nation Building School, on 2 September — and one particular slide really made me pause.
It challenged five common career beliefs:
❌ You must find the perfect career.
 ❌ You should do only one thing — one job function, company or industry — for the rest of your life.
 ❌ You should have your career figured out by a certain age.
 ❌ Your career must be based on your passion.
 ❌ Your career should always be fulfilling, fun and purposeful.
The reality?
A career is not a destination. It is an evolution.
Sometimes we discover our strengths after taking a job we didn't expect.
 Sometimes a career change is not starting over — it's bringing everything we've learned into a new direction.
 Sometimes our passion develops because we become good at something, rather than the other way around.
And perhaps most importantly, there is no expiry date on reinventing yourself.
Looking back at my own career journey across different industries and roles, I've come to appreciate that every experience adds another layer — even the ones that initially seemed unrelated.
So perhaps the better question isn't:
“What is my perfect career?”
but:
“What do I want to learn, contribute and become next?”
Thank you,Zaim Mohzani, for a thought-provoking session and for challenging some of the assumptions we often carry about our careers.
Which of these five career myths did you once believe?

Two of America’s most influential business leaders — Jamie Dimon and AT&T CEO John Stankey — recently shared advice on what it takes to build a successful career.

Four lessons stood out:
	1.	Work hard and deliver results. Your reputation is built on what you consistently bring to the table.
	2.	Keep learning. The people who continue developing their skills and expanding their perspective are better prepared when opportunities appear.
	3.	Build strong relationships. Careers aren’t built in isolation. Learn from others, seek mentors, and invest in genuine professional relationships.
	4.	Take ownership of your career. Don’t wait for someone else to map out your future. Be proactive about where you want to go and what you need to do to get there.

The common thread: career growth is rarely one big breakthrough. It’s the compound effect of consistently learning, delivering, connecting, and taking initiative.

Small improvements compound. So do good career decisions.

content:
What if your career isn’t a ladder to climb, but a jungle gym to explore?

For our Teachers’ Day Special, we had the privilege of hosting Debolina Dutta , Indian School of Business Professor, for a powerful conversation on Ikigai, strengths, purpose and navigating the twists and turns of our careers.

We often ask ourselves:
What should I do next?
Am I on the right career path?
What am I actually good at?
How do I build a career that feels meaningful?

This conversation offers a different way to look at these questions.

We explored:
✨ Ikigai — finding meaning at the intersection of what matters to us
✨ Strengths — recognising what we naturally bring to the table
✨ Career transitions — embracing change rather than fearing it
✨ The jungle gym mindset — seeing lateral moves, pivots and experiments as part of growth
✨ Purpose & fulfilment — going beyond titles and conventional definitions of success

What makes this episode especially meaningful is Prof. Debolina’s willingness to share her own experiences of navigating her career—making the conversation personal, honest and deeply relatable.

Perhaps the goal isn’t to find the perfect career path.

Perhaps it is to understand ourselves better, experiment, learn and keep moving towards work that feels meaningful.

content:
If I could talk to the 28-year-old me, I would tell her this…

You don’t need to have your entire career figured out at 28.

At that age, I thought I knew what my professional life would look like.

I was a pharmacist.

Years of studying.
Years of training.
A profession I was proud of.

Then I made a decision that felt quite scary at the time.

I changed direction.

From pharmacy into Islamic Financial Planning, Takaful & Legacy Planning.

Looking back after more than a decade in this industry, I’ve realised something:

Sometimes the biggest risk isn’t changing direction.

Sometimes it’s staying where you are simply because you’re afraid of what comes next.

But a career pivot doesn’t necessarily mean throwing everything away.

Today, I believe we can build on what we’ve already created while developing something new.

A new skill.
A new network.
A new income stream.
A new possibility.

And now, at 47, I see career development very differently.

Age doesn’t necessarily limit our possibilities.

Sometimes, it gives us something even more valuable:

Clarity.

Clarity about what matters.

What kind of life we want.

What we’re willing to learn.

And what we want to build for the future.

Perhaps that’s why I’m passionate today about helping other people explore their own possibilities too.

You don’t always have to leave what you’ve built.

Sometimes, you simply need to build alongside it.

One step at a time.

Biiznillah.

💚HudaHakim, IFP

content:
Sometimes, the most meaningful career shift happens before the job changes. 🌿
  
It happens when someone begins to see possibilities they hadn't considered before.
  
When the pieces between their education, experience, strengths and aspirations start connecting.
  
When “I'm not sure where I fit” slowly becomes “I can see where I could go.” ✨
  
🧩 Career clarity can feel a little like putting together a puzzle.
  
We often assume we're missing a piece,
  
🎓 Another qualification.
  
💡 Another skill.
  
💼 Another experience.
  
But sometimes, the pieces are already there.
  
We just haven't yet seen how they fit together.
  
That's what made this feedback from someone I had the privilege of working with especially meaningful to me. 💜
  
And it reminded me of something I deeply believe about career reinvention:
  
🪄 Before we keep searching for the missing piece, sometimes we need to step back and see the picture our existing pieces can create.
  
The experience.
  
The strengths.
  
The aspirations.
  
And sometimes, possibilities we simply couldn't see on our own.
  
Grateful to be part of career journeys like these! 🌿
  
#CareerReinvention #CareerDevelopment #CareerClarity #CareerConfidence #CareerTransition #WomenInCareers

content:
SOMETIMES A CAREER CHANGE STARTS LONG BEFORE SOMEONE LEAVES.

We often ask people:

“Why did you leave?”

It sounds like a simple question.

But it usually looks backward.

It asks for a reason.

A conflict.

A disappointment.

A better offer.

A resignation story.

I’m becoming more interested in another question:

What had you started noticing that made the previous direction no longer sufficient?

Because sometimes nothing dramatic happened.

The company did not collapse.

The role was not terrible.

The people were not necessarily wrong.

But the observer changed.

You started noticing a gap you could no longer ignore.

A problem nobody seemed interested in solving.

A capability you were no longer using.

A question that kept following you from meeting to meeting.

A tension between what the organization said and what actually happened.

A new curiosity.

A different definition of success.

And eventually, the old route could no longer contain what you were seeing.

That distinction matters.

A transition is not always an escape from something.

Sometimes it is evidence that your attention moved before your position did.

Looking back at my own trajectory, I can see this repeatedly.

I did not always know where I was going next.

But I often knew what I could no longer stop noticing.

That may be one reason non-linear careers make more sense in retrospect.

The jobs change.

The industries change.

The titles change.

But certain questions keep returning.

And eventually you realize:

maybe the trajectory was not built around positions.
Maybe it was built around attention.

This opens a new question I want to explore in Method 4K:

When someone changes direction, what signals appeared before the decision?

What were they noticing?

What had become insufficient?

What capability was trying to emerge?

What changed in the map before the person changed roads?

Because perhaps recalibration does not begin when we make a new decision.

It begins when the old reality stops explaining everything we are now able to see.

Method 4K | Observe the signal before judging the change.

VakıfBank’taki yaz stajımı tamamladığımı paylaşmaktan mutluluk duyuyorum. 💛

Bilgi Güvenlik Direktörlüğü, Süreç Yönetimi Ekibi’nde geçirdiğim bu süreçte; bilgi güvenliği yönetişimi, bankacılık bulgu süreçleri ve mevzuat uyumu üzerine çalışma fırsatı buldum. DORA kapsamındaki çalışmalara katkı sağlarken ISO 27001, ISO 27701, BYSEP ve BDDK gereklilikleri üzerine çalışmalar yürüttüm; aynı zamanda Archer tabanlı Durum sistemi ve dış denetim süreçlerini yakından tanıma fırsatı buldum.
Bunun yanında CIA prensipleri, IAM, SOC, risk yönetimi ve sızma testleri gibi bilgi güvenliğinin farklı alanlarında temel bilgiler edindim. Bu alanları farklı yönleriyle tanımak, bilgi güvenliğine ve süreç yönetimiyle olan ilişkisine daha bütüncül bir bakış geliştirmemi sağladı.
Bu süreç boyunca bilgi ve deneyimlerini paylaşan, sorularımı yanıtlayan ve gelişimime katkı sağlayan tüm ekip arkadaşlarıma ve yöneticilerime teşekkür ederim. Staj süresince aldığım değerli yönlendirmelerin, ilerleyen dönemde kariyer tercihlerimi şekillendirmeye devam edeceğine inanıyorum. Benim için hem mesleki hem de kişisel gelişim açısından önemli bir deneyim oldu.
Staj sürecim boyunca yol göstericiliği, desteği ve arkadaşlığı için Büşra Nur Karahan’a ayrıca teşekkür ederim. Kendisiyle çalışmak ve bu süreçte IT ve bankacılık sektöründeki deneyimlerini öğrenmek benim için oldukça kıymetliydi.

I’m happy to announce that I have completed my summer internship at VakıfBank. 💛

During my time with the Process Management Team within the Information Security Directorate, I had the opportunity to work on information security governance, banking finding processes, and regulatory compliance. I contributed to DORA-related work and studied ISO 27001, ISO 27701, BYSEP, and BDDK requirements, while also gaining firsthand insight into the Archer-based Durum system and external audit processes.
I also developed a foundational understanding of areas such as the CIA principles, IAM, SOC, risk management, and penetration testing. Exploring these different areas helped me develop a broader perspective on information security and its connection to process management.
I’m grateful to all my colleagues and managers who shared their knowledge, answered my questions, and supported me throughout this experience. I am certain that their invaluable guidance throughout my internship will continue to shape my future career decisions. It was a valuable step in both my professional and personal development.
A special thanks to Büşra Nur Karahan for her attentive guidance, constant support, and friendship throughout my internship. I’m truly grateful for everything I learned from you and for making this experience even more meaningful.

Today, we are genuinely proud to see those efforts pay off. Having our work recognized with a Stevie Award, and seeing that we have built products that have real value and impact in the industry, has been an incredibly rewarding experience.

Once again, a huge thank you to all my managers and colleagues who contributed to this journey.

English below.

TR:
Yapay zeka güvenliği artık sadece prompt injection veya model davranışı tartışması değil.

CISA’nın 2 Eylül’de KEV kataloğuna eklediği yeni zafiyetler arasında LiteLLM ve Starlette gibi AI/LLM altyapılarında sık karşılaştığımız bileşenler de var.

LiteLLM’deki CVE-2026-59822, geçersiz bir Bearer token üzerinden MCP oturumu kurulmasına ve bağlı araçlara yetkisiz erişime imkan verebiliyor. Starlette’deki CVE-2026-48710 ise Host header işleme biçiminden kaynaklanan bir güvenlik kontrolü atlatma problemi oluşturuyor.

Bence burada asıl önemli nokta şu: AI sistemlerinin attack surface’i sadece modele gönderilen prompt’tan oluşmuyor.

MCP sunucuları, API gateway’ler, orchestration katmanları, framework’ler, agent servisleri, secret management ve bağlı servislerin tamamı artık AI security değerlendirmesinin parçası olmak zorunda.

Klasik web pentest yaklaşımını AI sistemlerine uygulamak tek başına yeterli değil. Model katmanı ile altyapı güvenliğini birlikte test etmek gerekiyor.

En:
AI security is no longer just about prompt injection or model behavior.

Among the vulnerabilities CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 2 are components commonly found in AI and LLM infrastructure, including LiteLLM and Starlette.

CVE-2026-59822 in LiteLLM can allow an unauthenticated attacker to establish an MCP session using an arbitrary Bearer token and access connected MCP tools. CVE-2026-48710 in Starlette can allow security controls based on request paths to be bypassed through malformed Host headers.

The bigger point is that the attack surface of an AI system extends far beyond the prompt.

MCP servers, API gateways, orchestration layers, frameworks, agent services, secrets and downstream integrations all need to be part of an AI security assessment.

Traditional web application testing is still essential, but it is no longer sufficient on its own. AI systems need to be assessed as complete architectures.

#CyberSecurity #AISecurity #LLMSecurity #MCP #VulnerabilityManagement #Pentest

content:
Bir yapay zeka modeli yanlış sonuç verdiğinde, sorumlu kim?
Üretici mi? Laboratuvar mı? Klinik biyokimya uzmanı mı?

YZ laboratuvar pratiğine hızla giriyor; regülasyonlar bazen kapasitenin bile önüne geçiyor. 

Ama asıl soru şu: Laboratuvarlarımız bu modelleri gerçekten doğrulayacak ve klinik olarak izleyebilecek kapasiteye sahip mi?
Yakın zamanlı bir ankette;
 klinik biyokimya uzmanlarının %70'inin bu iş için bir SOP'u,  
 %83,5'inin ise eğitimli personelinin olmadığı görünüyor. (çıktıların        sorumluluğu çoktan uzmana verilmişken.)
Kurallar hazırlığın önüne geçtiğinde ortaya çıkan şeyi mektubumuzda "kağıt üzerinde uyum" olarak adlandırıyoruz: kutu işaretlenir, ama arkasındaki iş büyük ölçüde şekilden ibaret kalır.

Bu açığı ve olası çözüm yollarını CCLM'de yayımlanan mektubumuzda tartışıyoruz. 👇


Who's responsible when an AI model gets it wrong?
The manufacturer? The lab? The clinical biochemistry specialist?
AI is moving into laboratory practice fast — and regulation is sometimes moving even faster, ahead of what labs can actually handle. But the real question is: are our laboratories actually equipped to validate these models and monitor them clinically?
In a recent survey of clinical biochemistry professionals, 70% had no SOP in place for it, and 83.5% had no trained staff — even as responsibility for the outputs already sits with the specialist.
We call what happens when rules outpace readiness "paper compliance": the box gets ticked, but the work behind it is largely nominal.
We discuss this gap — and what might close it — in our new Letter published in CCLM. 👇

#ArtificialIntelligence #AIinHealthcare #LaboratoryMedicine #ClinicalChemistry #MedicalAI #DigitalHealth #LaboratoryDiagnostics #CCLM
Osman Oğuz Deniz İlhan Topcu

content:
Ankara Seramik A.S bünyesindeki staj dönemimi tamamladım.
Bu süreç bana mühendisliğin sadece ofiste ekrana bakıp teorik hesap yapmaktan ibaret olmadığını çok net gösterdi. Sahaya inip işin mutfağına girmeden mühendis olunamayacağını; yeri geldiğinde bir teknisyen gibi kablo çekip pano montajı yapmayı, yeri geldiğinde ise mühendis gözüyle sürece müdahale etmeyi gerektirdiğini bizzat deneyimledim. Aynı zamanda ham çamurdan başlayıp kV’lar mertebesindeki yüksek gerilime dayanan porselen izolatörlerin üretimindeki tüm proseslere baştan sona şahit olmak vizyonumu fazlasıyla genişletti.

Staj süresince edindiğim pratik tecrübenin yanında fabrikadaki operasyonel bir eksiğe de doğrudan çözüm üretme fırsatım oldu. Tesiste reaktif enerji oranlarının ve ceza sınırlarının manuel takip edilmesi veri dağınıklığı yaratıyordu. Bu süreci dijitalleştirmek adına yapay zeka araçlarından da destek alarak Python tabanlı bir masaüstü takip arayüzü geliştirdim. Uygulama ile vardiya bazlı endüktif/kapasitif verileri düzenli kayıt altına alıp yasal ceza sınırlarını grafik üzerinden anlık izlenebilir hale getirdik.
Kısacası hem sahada donanım ve elektrik işlerinin tozunu yuttuğum hem de arkada kod yazarak sürece somut katkı sağladığım, laf kalabalığı olmayan verimli bir dönem oldu. 

Süreç boyunca tecrübelerini paylaşan tüm Ankara Seramik ekibine ve Ahmet Altun'a teşekkürler.

En:
I have completed my internship at Ankara Seramik A.S.
This experience clearly demonstrated that engineering goes far beyond running theoretical calculations in an office. Getting hands-on in the field is essential; I learned firsthand that you often need to pull cables and wire control panels like a technician, while stepping back to look at the bigger picture as an engineer. Witnessing the complete manufacturing process—from raw clay to porcelain insulators capable of withstanding tens of kilovolts (kV)—was also an invaluable experience.

Alongside gaining practical field experience, I had the opportunity to solve a day-to-day operational issue on the shop floor. Tracking reactive energy consumption and statutory penalty limits manually was causing unstructured data. To digitalize this workflow, I developed a Python desktop application with the assistance of AI tools. The software logs shift-based inductive and capacitive rates, enabling real-time graphical monitoring against penalty thresholds. Overall, it was a productive and practical period where I both handled shop floor hardware and delivered a software solution. 

Sincere thanks to the entire Ankara Seramik team and Ahmet Altun for their guidance throughout this journey.

content:
Bir liderin değeri, odadayken değil; odada yokken anlaşılır.
Toplantıya girdiğinde herkes yönünü liderden alıyorsa, bu ilk bakışta güçlü liderlik gibi görünebilir.
Ama bazen tam tersidir.
Çünkü güçlü liderlik, her kararda merkeze oturmak değildir.
Ekibin lider olmadan da doğru soruları sorabilmesini, önceliklendirebilmesini ve karar verebilmesini sağlamaktır.
Bunun için üç şey gerekir:
Karar sınırlarının net olması.
Hata yapmanın cezalandırılmaması.
Ve liderin her boşluğu kendi fikriyle doldurmaması.
Bir ekip sürekli liderine bakıyorsa, lider çok görünür olabilir.
Ama organizasyon hala ona bağımlıdır.
Liderliğin en güçlü çıktısı, bağımlılık değil; karar verme kapasitesidir.
İyi liderler sadece sonuç üretmez.
Kendileri olmadan da sonuç üretebilen sistemler kurar.
---------------
You understand the quality of a leader not when they are in the room, but when they are not.
If everyone looks to the leader before making a decision, it can look like strong leadership.
Sometimes, it is the opposite.
Strong leadership is not about staying at the center of every decision.
It is about building a team that can ask the right questions, set priorities, and make sound decisions without you.
That requires three things:
Clear decision boundaries.
Room to make mistakes.
And a leader who does not fill every silence with their own answer.
If a team constantly needs the leader, the leader may be highly visible.
But the organization is still dependent.
The real output of leadership is not control.
It is decision-making capacity.
Good leaders do not just produce results.
They build systems that can produce results without them.

#Leadership #DecisionMaking #OrganizationalDesign #Management #FutureOfWork

LEADERSHIP
Leadership is not the art of being the strongest person in the room; it is the art of making the room stronger. Research supports this idea: empowering leadership is positively associated with performance, creativity and organizational citizenship.  leader who always gives the answer creates followers; a leader who teaches people how to find the answer creates capability. A manager who takes every difficult negotiation may look successful, but the manager who develops five people capable of negotiating has created something that lasts beyond himself. Perhaps the deepest measure of leadership is simple: 
when you leave the room, are people weaker without you—or stronger because of you?

Liderlik, oradaki en güçlü kişi olmak değil;  herkesi daha güçlü hâle getirebilmektir. Araştırmalar da güçlendirici liderliğin performans, yaratıcılık ve çalışanların olumlu katkılarıyla ilişkili olduğunu gösteriyor.  Her sorunun cevabını veren lider, kendisine bağımlı insanlar yetiştirir; cevabı bulmayı öğreten lider ise kapasite yaratır. Her zor pazarlığı kendisi yapan yönetici başarılı görünebilir; fakat beş kişiye iyi pazarlık yapmayı öğreten yönetici, kendisinden sonra da yaşayacak bir güç bırakır. Belki liderliğin en derin ölçüsü şudur: 
**Sen oradan çıktığında insanlar eksiliyor mu, yoksa senin sayende daha güçlü mü kalıyor?**

content:
Kişisel, ülkem ve tüm meslektaşlarım adına gurur duyduğum bir gelişmeyi sizlerle paylaşmak isterim. Dünyada benzeri olmayan OPS kitabında yazımın çıkması mutluluk verici. Verilen emek ve özveriyi bildiğim için, umarım çok fazla arkadaşımın da böyle yazıları çıkar. 

Bu yazıyı yazarken 30 yıllık ve birçok sektörde elde edilen tecrübeyi nasıl bir sayfada aktarabileceğim konusunda çok düşündüm. 

Dünya çapında 160’tan fazla düşünür, CEO, yasa koyucu, akademisyen, psikolog, endüstri liderleri, ön saha uygulayıcılarının arasında benim de sesimin duyulması mesleki olarak anlatması kolay olmayan büyük bir onur.

2020 yılında iş kazaları ve meslek hastalıklarından dünyada 2.78 milyon insan öldü. Bugün artan teknoloji ve imkanlara rağmen bu sayı 2.93 milyona ulaştı. 
Yasalara, sistemlere ve on yıllarca süren çabalardan bağımsız olarak, bugün hala iş kazaları ve meslek hastalıkları can almaya devam ediyor. Ekonomik boyutu da trilyonlarca doları geçiyor.

Bu kitap bir teknik İSG manueli değil.
Bu bir liderlik manifestosu.

İSG’nin performansın bir parçası olduğuna inanmıyorum; İSG performansın bir çarpanı.

Güvenli işyerleri daha dayanıklı.
Birbirine güvenen takımlar daha üretken.
Önem verme kültürü her zaman önemsizleştiren kültürlerden daha başarılı.

I’d like to share a development that makes me proud personally, for my country, and for all of my colleagues. Having my article published in the OPS book, a truly unique global publication is a great source of happiness for me. Knowing the level of effort and dedication behind all the work, I sincerely hope many more friends and colleagues will have their voices featured in similar ways.

While writing this article, I spent a lot of time thinking about how to distill 30 years of experience across multiple industries into a single page. 

Being heard among more than 160 global thinkers, CEOs, policymakers, academics, psychologists, industry leaders, and frontline practitioners is not something easy to describe professionally, but it is an incredible honor.

In 2020, 2.78 million people around the world lost their lives due to occupational accidents and diseases. Despite today’s advanced technologies and capabilities, this number has risen to 2.93 million. Regardless of laws, systems, and decades of effort, workplace accidents and occupational illnesses continue to claim lives, with an economic impact reaching trillions of dollars.

This book is not a technical OHS manual. 
It is a leadership manifesto.

I don’t believe OHS is just a part of performance; I believe OHS is a multiplier of performance.

Safe workplaces are more resilient. 
Teams built on trust are more productive. 
A culture of care will always outperform a culture of disregard.

content:
Leadership is not about getting it right every time.

One idea from Jim Brown’s “The Imperfect CEO” stayed with me:

Intent ≠ Impact.

We may lead with the best intentions. Yet leadership is ultimately experienced through the impact we create — on trust, ownership, dialogue and performance.

My reflection is that this is also part of strategic maturity: remaining curious enough to listen, self-aware enough to question our assumptions, and adaptable enough to learn when our impact differs from our intention.

Perhaps leadership maturity is less about becoming a “perfect” leader — and more about remaining a learning leader.

A thoughtful read and a valuable reminder.

Inspired by Jim Brown’s The Imperfect CEO (2026). Personal reflections are my own.

—

Liderlik, her seferinde doğruyu yapmak ya da tüm cevaplara sahip olmak değil.

Jim Brown’ın “The Imperfect CEO” kitabından bende kalan güçlü fikirlerden biri:

Niyet ≠ Etki.

Niyetimiz ne kadar iyi olursa olsun, liderlik aslında yarattığımız etkiyle anlam kazanıyor — güven, sorumluluk alma, diyalog ve performans üzerindeki etkimizle.

Benim için bu aynı zamanda stratejik olgunluğun da bir parçası: dinleyecek kadar meraklı, kendi varsayımlarımızı sorgulayacak kadar öz farkındalıklı ve yarattığımız etki niyetimizden farklı olduğunda öğrenip uyum sağlayacak kadar esnek kalabilmek.

Belki de liderlikte olgunlaşmak, “mükemmel” bir lider olmaya çalışmaktan çok, öğrenmeye devam eden bir lider kalabilmek.

Düşündüren ve kendimize dönüp bakmayı hatırlatan değerli bir kitap.

Jim Brown’ın The Imperfect CEO (2026) kitabından ilhamla. Kişisel değerlendirmeler bana aittir.

The hardest part of #leadership isn't giving someone the opportunity to reach high.

​It's standing completely still while they outreach you.

To hold someone up that high, you have to accept two brutal truths:

• ​From the outside, they look taller than you.

​You're capping them.

​The ultimate test of a leader isn't how much talent you attract.

​It’s how much talent you can tolerate being surpassed by.
